Whether this restrains spending or allows it to expand depends on how it is designed. If the envelope is capped, eligibility is clearly defined, duration is limited, and a repayment source is specified, it would work as a disciplined carve‑out. Without those constraints, it risks becoming additional spending under a new label. The risk is that multi‑year budgeting without execution oversight leads to waste rather than better allocation. Test 2: Supplementary budget discipline The second test is the restriction on the use of supplementary budgets. The proposal calls for limiting them to genuinely urgent items, and its effectiveness depends on how “urgency” is defined. Recent supplementary budgets have routinely included recurring measures that would normally sit in the initial budget. If such items continue to be routed through supplementary budgets under a broad definition of urgency, the change amounts to relabeling. If, instead, they are folded into the initial budget baseline or reclassified into the investment envelope, the framework would operate as intended. One caveat is timing. Concentration, Profits, and the Competitive Landscape Ahead of AI Disruption AI has the potential both to intensify competition by eroding the advantages of today’s dominant incumbents and to reduce it by enabling the most successful AI adopters to pull far ahead. Its impact will depend not only on how competitive the AI industry itself proves to be but also on the status quo it disrupts. In this week’s Analyst, we take a closer look at why concentration and profit margins have risen to historically elevated levels (Exhibit 1), how closely the two trends are linked, and what the competitive backdrop looks like in sectors where AI is likely to have the largest impact. The Long-Run Rise in Corporate Concentration New data spanning nearly a century of tax and administrative records document a long-run rise in corporate concentration across the US and other advanced economies. Drawing on the IRS Statistics of Income data for the US and on VAT and sales tax records, corporate tax filings, and company registries for other countries, economist Yueran Ma and co-authors have constructed sales, asset, equity capital, and net income shares of top firms as standardized cross-country measures of concentration.1 As shown in Exhibit 2, the sales share of the top 1% of US firms rose from roughly 60% in the 1960s-70s to around 80% in recent years. Secondary demand effects via export channels were barely visible, though elevated prices and heightened uncertainty did weigh on domestic consumption and capex. Stagflation risks are rising. Headline figures, especially in nominal terms, should hold up on the back of the PPI beat. But the divergence within the economy is still getting entrenched, and import-led reflation added a new layer to the divide: upstream price and profitability improvements have not translated into investment or capex amid supply shocks, while downstream sectors embraced a further demand hit — as shown in April's data. Fading policy support has compounded the pressure. Policy adjustments could start now. Fiscal deployment is likely to accelerate in our view, with bond issuance, infrastructure spending, and the use of RMB800bn policy-financing tools for this year. The bar for an outright budget revision remains high in our view. The PPI reflation complicates the PBoC’s policy calculation. For markets, two questions will underlay the 'Manchesterism' agenda. Number 1: the cost. 'Manchesterism' would represent more up-front spending – both in terms of day-to-day spending and capex spending. Taxes will also play a role, with some of the Labour left still talking up the idea of 'wealth taxes'. Indeed, given the likely market reaction to a more active fiscal policy stance, we think more tax rises will sit at the heart of 'Manchesterism' in redistributing income/wealth. The key here will be how a pivot to the soft-left would shift the fiscal framework – this will determine the balance between spending and taxation, and ultimately borrowing. But to be sure, the higher the price tag for 'Manchesterism', the bigger the compensation investors will require for fiscal spending. Number 2: growth. With medium/long gilt yields having crossed 5% already, such fiscal intervention could be justified if accompanied by a genuine growth resurgence. At face value, 'Manchesterism' has seemingly engineered a growth recovery in Greater Manchester. Positioning – Mildly Bearish ICE weekly aggregate positioning data as of 12-May-2026 show asset managers holding net long positions of around 350,000 contracts, with leveraged funds net short by around 210,000 contracts (see Exhibit 2 ). The leveraged-fund short position is consistent with continued long-basis positioning, although the latest data points suggest some unwinding, likely driven by rising domestic volatility (see Exhibit 3 ). Asset-manager net longs have fallen by around 65,000 contracts since 27-Feb-2026 (see Exhibit 3 ), but remain elevated relative to the available history since ICE began publishing weekly aggregate positioning for long gilt futures and options in late March 2025. Combined with elevated open interest, this positioning profile has mildly bearish implications for the roll into first notice day on 28-May-2026. Anecdotal evidence and investor discussions suggest directional positioning remains skewed long, while elevated global and domestic uncertainty could encourage asset managers to bring forward roll activity rather than wait. Given their long-futures exposure, accelerated roll activity from asset managers could exert downward pressure on the M6/ U6 roll into first notice day. The new regulation marginally strengthens our bearish view on the domestic curve, as we anticipate policymakers could be forced to hike rates due to upward inflation pressures from higher fuel prices, a resurgence in domestic demand, and the imminent risk of a food - price shock associated with a possible “Super Niño” event. We now forecast 50bp of rate hikes in the second half of 2026. To reflect our upside view we paid 2y Camara against the US to dampen volatility amid ongoing Middle - East uncertainty (see EM rates: Entering 2y Camara - US spread payer ). We continue to believe that any compression of that spread would provide a better opportunity to add to payer positions, from a more attractive entry level (Figure 5). When we compare the current exposure to the Maximum Derivative Exposure Limit and adopt a worst-case scenario for AFPs’ holdings of rate derivatives (a parallel 40bp sell-off in rates), the aggregate net loss from both domestic and foreign rate contracts would amount to roughly USD8.6bn, or c. 3.4 % of total AUM (Figure 4). Because the LED ceiling ranges from 2% to 3% of AUM depending on the fund category, our analysis suggests that AFPs probably will rebalance their holdings. A strong focus on BESS has overshadowed weak EV sales, and positive headlines on the storage sector have only increased since the Middle East conflict upended energy markets and highlighted an urgent need for renewables and BESS buildout to support a shift away from fossil fuel dependence. The real-world implications for BESS will depend on how individual countries assess their long-term energy security and their ability to ramp up renewables, but we think the current sentiment boost should be enough to sustain strong upstream (over)production of cathodes and continued strong demand, especially for lithium carbonate used in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries . LFP battery production for EVs and BESS in China has shown no sign of slowing (up 52% y/y in Q1 according to CABIA), while sales surged 112% y/y, indicating continued downstream demand and flexibility to build stockpiles. We therefore see prices supported at high-USD20/kg levels in the near term. records.text: China Economics 18 May 2026 Citi Research 2 China's growth momentum slowed sharply in April. Both supply and demand indicators missed expectations by a wide margin, hitting or approaching post- Covid lows. Industrial production grew just 4.1% YoY — the weakest reading since mid-2023 (Citi/Mkt: 5.7%/6.0%), a notable disappointment given the strong export beat earlier in the month. Domestic demand fell short of already-subdued expectations after the sharp miss in credit data. Retail sales rose a mere 0.2% YoY in April, a new low since 2023 (Citi/Mkt: 1.0%/2.0%), while cumulative fixed asset investment (FAI) turned negative at -1.6% YoY Ytd (Citi/Mkt: +1.5/+1.7%YoY Ytd), implying a monthly rate of -8.0% YoY. With the beat in both CPI and PPI, real growth could be negative for retail sales, and close to -10%YoY for investment. Underlying weakness in the K-shaped economy was revealed further and Mideast conflict impact surfaced. Reduced trade-in subsidies knocked roughly 2ppts off headline retail sales; infrastructure investment turned negative at - 3.0%YoY in April, and property investment continue to deteriorate despite green shoots. The new economy remained a bright spot, particularly on the supply side. On Mideast impact, direct supply-side disruptions appear limited: output of petrochemical products (ethylene, sulfuric acid) turned negative at -2% to -4% YoY in April. This resilience was driven primarily by exports of auto and AI-related products . Auto exports surged by 44.2% y/y in April, while shipments of integrated circuits and computer components jumped by 99.6% and 47.3% y/y, respectively. Together, these three categories contributed more than 10pp to overall export growth. Although China's exports to the Middle East fell by roughly 43.3% y/y in April, the decline was more than offset by strong growth elsewhere. Exports to non-US markets roseby 14.2% y/y, with shipments to the EU, ASEAN and South Korea increasing by13.4%,15.2% and 24.6% y/y, respectively. In addition, exports to the US returned to positive territory, up 11.3% y/y, due to a favourable base effect. China’s imports jumped by 25.3% y/y, compared with the 22.8% y/y increase in Q1. The surge was not curbed by weaker commodity volumes because price gains more than offset the decline in quantities. records.text: Keng Goh Macro Strategy Team 18 May 2026 Classification: Premium Material 1 Insights Information Classification: General FX Execution Insights – Global bond selloff deepens in G10 rates Figure 1: FX and rates vol seemingly contained, but trend higher Figure 2: Volume (5-day, percentiles) Weekly Insights: A broad risk-off move across FX and rates spilled into equities, pausing the AI-led rally. The global bond selloff accelerated following firm US and Japanese price data, reinforcing sticky inflation concerns amid elevated oil prices. Gilts underperformed amid renewed political uncertainty, with 10 - year yields surpassing 2022 “mini - budget” levels, echoed by Treasuries at highs since 2023. Whilst FX volatility has moderated and bond inflation premia appears stretched, these cross -asset dynamics continue to shape liquidity and options pricing. Volume: Trading activit y reverted to a familiar divergence , as G10 volumes moderated substantially from top decile to bottom quartile, while EM volumes rebounded, driven by thinning liquidity in DM commodity pairs and USDTRY. Depth of Book: USDJPY and aggregate EM order book s reached year highs supported by intervention risks and dollar weakness, although the DXY showed signs of reprieve, rising above 99 for the fist time this month. Spreads: Against an otherwise steady backdrop, USDTRY and USDJPY stood out last week, tightening below long run DM & EM averages we track. records.text: Sven Jari Stehn +44(20)7774-8061 | jari.stehn@gs.com Goldman Sachs International European Views: Testing Times 18 May 2026 | 3:44AM BST 1. Euro area growth looks set to cool significantly this year. Our commodity team’s forecast remains for a gradual normalisation of energy supply by the summer, pushing down oil and gas prices steadily towards year-end. But we expect the level of energy prices to remain materially higher than before the war, implying a significant headwind to Euro area consumption and investment. Following a disappointing 0.1% in Q1, we look for similarly slow growth in Q2-Q4, with risks skewed towards stagnation (or even contraction) if energy prices remain higher than anticipated. Investors should consider this report as only a single factor in making their investment decision. records.text: 6% at month-end as index- driven rebalancing amplifies activity. • This link runs through two channels. First, new supply triggers immediate repositioning along the issuer curve such as selling off-the-runs and buying the on-the-run. Second, the new deal itself trades actively, with investors topping up allocations from primary or selling to capture the new-issue concessions, driving two-way flows. • Secondary volumes of new issues peak after issuance, and again at month-end. Post- issuance turnover tops out at around 10% with the tightest bid-offer (5-8bp). Activity then fades during the month, before rebounding at month-end, when turnover rises to 4-5% and the bid-offer tightens to 11bp. • We find early evidence that new issues enter ETF create baskets shortly after issuance, ahead of index inclusion. First, daily ETF holdings track the arrival of new bonds almost one- for-one. Second, first-month TRACE flows are consistently skewed to net client selling, in sizes that closely match reported ETF ownership. We argue this 'imbalance' reflects ETF create activity – which is not captured in TRACE – and is best interpreted as implicit buy flows. • Finally, index extension remains a powerful and predictable technical driver of near- term IG performance. Heavy issuance leads to large index extensions, pushing duration higher as new issues enter and short bonds roll out, typically followed by tightening in subsequent months. records.text: have become increasingly volatile over the past few months, driven by the Middle East conflict and a weakening KRW. This led to rapid increases in front-end rates and the market pricing in nearly five policy-rate hikes from the BoK over the next year at its peak. Despite some retracement, the market is still pricing in around four rate hikes from the BoK over the next year. The uncertainty around the BoK's future actions, volatility in the currency, and the transmission of inflationary risks are contributing to the persistent volatility in rates. Although we expect the BoK to implement only two rate hikes (see South Korea: Implications of higher growth and inflation, dated 27 April), front-end rates may remain elevated relative to fundamentals, in our view, due to the ongoing AI cycle and risk of higher inflation amid elevated energy prices. As such, we prefer to pay front-end rates on dips, such as the 1y1y rate at 3.45%, or receive the very short-end if markets price in an extreme number of hikes, such as the 1y rate at 3.35%. We also remain bullish on the KRW over the medium term, despite its vulnerability to high energy prices. We expect the currency to outperform its peers due to portfolio inflows, retail repatriation, and flows from the WGBI and the NPS. As the KRW appreciates, this should alleviate some pressure on front-end KRW rates. We remain more bullish on long-end rates, particularly because of the gradual inclusion of KTBs in the WGBI. This impact is relatively modest when compared with the stress losses observed in interest rate derivatives. While AFPs could unwind non-hedging FX derivatives to meet the LED requirement if needed, the extent of change in the overall FX derivative portfolio is unclear. AFPs may still expand hedging activity, and the liquidity ratio requirement could also affect these positions – a factor that is difficult to assess because detailed public data is unavailable. AFPs’ FX activity takes a back seat in USDCLP and the cross-currency basis: In the short run, we expect AFPs’ activity to have only a modest effect on the CLP exchange rate and the CLP basis. Over the medium term, however, increased FX hedging by AFPs could push USDCLP lower and compress the CLP basis. Since AFPs own a large share of foreign assets, their hedging choices affect both the CLP and the cross-currency basis (see CLP: Further underperformance likely in medium term, dated 24 February 2024). An increase in the AFP hedging ratio would support the CLP, lower FX points and compress the CLP basis (see Chile: Pension fund hedging shift to stabilize CLP basis, dated 17 September 2025). The question is less about any single print and more about whether cumulative evidence challenges the FOMC’s baseline. Tolerance to “look through” elevated prints would ultimately hinge on credibility. As with inflation expectations, the Committee is likely to become more sensitive to upside risks as the disturbance lengthens and broadens. Three scenarios We see three broad scenarios that could plausibly trigger a hawkish turn by the FOMC, even with Kevin Warsh now at the helm as Fed Chair. 1. Signs that longer-term inflation expectations are becoming unanchored In our view, the most direct path to hikes would be evidence that longer-term inflation expectations are at risk of becoming unanchored. Such evidence would involve one or both of the following, listed by importance: • A sustained rise in market 5-10 year inflation breakevens, particularly if moves are disorderly or decoupled from near-term inflation dynamics, • Broadening evidence across survey-based measures (eg, Michigan, New York Fed) that longer- run expectations are drifting higher. The common thread linking these indicators is the signals they provide about where annualized inflation is likely to settle once supply pressures have worked their way through market prices. As Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham piloted a push towards technical training in an effort to build localised skills fit for industry. His response to up-skill Greater Manchester was to establish the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate (MBacc) – a technical qualification developed with local employers to provide a credible alternative to the university route. The goal is to make such a route available in every Greater Manchester school and college by 2030, with pathways linked to the city-region's priority growth sectors: advanced manufacturing, green technology, digital, and life sciences. Why is this important? Burnham has described the MBacc as "aspirational socialism" — redistributive in intent but designed to create opportunity, not just redistribute income. In essence, Burnham sees devolving post-16 skills funding to city regions, and linking it to local labour-market demand as the structural fix to the skills shortages faced up and down the country. Even if fuel subsidies remain in place, we expect second- round effects to eventually filter through, putting upward pressure on inflation over time, via other parts of the economy and neighboring countries. We also think the fiscal costs of maintaining subsidies are underappreciated – they have surged from MYR700mn a month (pre-conflict) to an estimated MYR7bn in April. A potential larger dividend payment from Petronas could provide some fiscal offset, but we do not think it justifies long-end MYR rates trading near pre-conflict levels and believe the curve should be steeper. With the front end pricing in almost no rate hikes, we see little value in receiving it, and prefer to express our view of a steeper curve via an outright paid position in 5y swaps (see EM rates: Pay 5y MYR rates, dated 23 April). The second hypothesis points to weaker antitrust enforcement and higher regulatory barriers to entry. For example, economists Germán Gutiérrez and Thomas Philippon have argued that the rise in occupational licensing requirements has raised the fixed costs of starting new businesses, deterring entry by competitors.3 While this channel has plausibly played some role, the evidence on its quantitative importance remains inconclusive. Using the Department of Justice Antitrust Division’s budget as a proxy for enforcement intensity, we find that concentration has risen at a broadly similar pace across different US antitrust regimes since the 1960s (Exhibit 4). Evidence from Europe also suggests that while stricter merger enforcement is associated with lower concentration, this relationship has weakened over time.4 We view the third hypothesis—that new technologies have enabled a small number of firms to leverage economies of scale and capture larger market shares—as the most compelling. Notably, MYR rates have remain relatively muted throughout the oil shock, with the front-end not pricing any rate hikes like its regional peers and the curve (e.g., 2s10s) flattening for most of the conflict. While we emphathize with these moves to some extent, owing to Malaysia’s status as a net energy exporter and capped fuel prices, we think that current levels are too low, and the curve is too flat. Even if fuel subsidies remain in place, we expect second- round effects to eventually filter through, putting upward pressure on inflation over time, via other parts of the economy and neighboring countries. Furthermore, we think that the fiscal costs of maintaining these subsidies are underappreciated, as subsidy costs have surged from MYR700mn/month (pre-conflict) to an estimated MYR7bn in April. While a potentially larger dividend payment from Petronas could provide some fiscal offset, we do not think it justifies long-end MYR rates trading near pre-conflict levels, and the curve should be steeper. With the front-end is pricing almost no rate hikes, we think there is little value in receiving it, and prefer to express our view of a steeper curve via an outright paid position in 5y swaps (see EM rates: Pay 5y MYR rates, dated 23 April). The appeal of long bond carry trades has also waned in recent months, as implied yields have surged across Asia, eroding potential gains from funding long bond positions with implied yields.

Although Singapore’s fiscal year runs from April to March, the MAS releases its auction and issuance calendar by calendar year, typically in October or November of the previous year. It also publishes separate issuance calendars for MAS Bills and Floating Rate Notes (FRNs) semi-annually, in May and November. Unlike many other economies, Singapore often runs budget surpluses (Figure 9), which gives the MAS flexibility to adjust its auction sizes based on its assessment of what the market needs. The MAS can also conduct ad hoc mini-auctions or bond syndications if it deems them necessary. Bond curve seasonality: Auctions are typically held once a month, at month-end, with issuance taking place at the start of the next month, with typically very few auctions at the end of the year i.e., November/December. records.text: cy of companies). Exchange rate fluctuations tend to affect assets and liabilities – and hence the NIIP – unevenly. Eurozone cross-border assets are mostly denominated in foreign currency (above all dollars), while cross border liabilities are mainly dominated in euros. As a result, exchange rate movements tend to affect external assets more than liabilities. An appreciation of the euro lowers the value (in euro) of external assets more than external liabilities and hence leads to a decrease in net assets. (1) More broadly, then, euro appreciation tends to worsen the EZ's NIIP , while euro depreciation tends to improve it. At the end of 2025, the Eurozone net international investment position amounted to €1.76 trillion, moderately up in nominal terms from €1.75 trillion in Q4-24. Relative to GDP , however, the NIIP was down from 11.5% to 11.1%. Between Q4-24 and Q4-25, the euro appreciated against the dollar (from an average 1.07 in Q4-24 to 1.16 in Q4- 25), which – other things equal – lowered the value of foreign assets in €-terms). Net international investment position (NIIP) measures the EZ's net claims (net liabilities) vis-à-vis the rest of the world Euro appreciation (depreciation) tends to worsen (improve) the Eurozone's NIIP 1. According to Fastmarkets, in the three months to end-February, just 7.8kt of cobalt was cleared for export in the DRC under the new quota system. Notably, China’s huge Jianxiawo mine remains suspended at the time of writing with no news on a potential reopening or on the award of a new permit. We think a restart is likely around July/August this year, assuming a 12-month process . The Jiangxi Ministry of Natural Resources published in April official assessment reports for the Huaqiao Dagang, Huashan, Dingxing and Tongan lepidolite mines, sparking speculation that all four may be required to halt production in May and go through formal procedures to obtain official lepidolite mining licenses. This would take out roughly 5% of annual lithium production and has rattled the market despite the lack of any official comments thus far. records.text: 18 May 2026 UK Blog Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG Pillar #1: Devolution as the fundamental backbone to national growth We start by stating the obvious: perhaps the biggest reason for Greater Manchester's success story is in devolution. Indeed, devolution sits at the heart of 'Manchesterism'. It is, in truth, the operating system behind some of the headline success seen in the last decade or so. In a Centre for Cities report (2025), Burnham argued that devolution has "helped reverse a century-long trend towards political centralisation," describing the model as "future-facing, long-term, bottom-up, collaborative, innovative and ambitious." Looking at Greater Manchester, it's easy to note the various success points of devolution. In 2011/2012, the UK agreed to an ambitious City Deal with Greater Manchester. In 2014, the Government established the Greater Manchester Agreement – which included the transition to a directly elected Mayor. In 2016, Greater Manchester benefited from a further ambitious 'Growth Deal'. And in 2023, the Trailblazer Deal gave Greater Manchester enhanced powers over education, housing, and transport — more than any English city outside London. The argument across the various devolution stamps was simple: local leaders know their economies better than Whitehall does. We note that any signs of production cuts as the conflict persists would likely lead to market stress and rising prices given an increasing reliance on Indonesia's MHPproduction . Bullish outlook: With no easing of DRC export restrictions in sight, delays in cobalt shipments and increasing supply risks, we remain bullish. We see upside risks especially in Q3 (when metals inventories are expected to be depleted), unless the market sees faster, smoother exports out of the DRC and/or a rapid resumption of sulphur flows in a late-Q2 de-escalation scenario as set out in Energy: Potential for de-escalation but upside risks remain,dated 9 April. Any influx of backlogged supply in H2 2026 would however work to cap price upside, with prices then stabilising around the USD26/lb level, although we think it more likely that supply continues to be pushed out in the near term as firms take time to align with the more complex export procedures . They have struggled to maintain their outperformance into 2026 and we see key vulnerabilities in the coming months that reflect tactical downside risks. Regime: Banks do best (relative to market) in the early and mid parts of a cycle. We had expected a new late-cycle acceleration this year and had kept them as a favoured sector as a result. That acceleration is no longer being forecast and the composite leading indicator has slipped into slowdown - typically when banks begin to underperform. Debt and IIP data offer different perspectives – we see them as complements rather than substitutes in identifying potential vulnerabilities from excessive debt. The debt data leaves out assets; i.e. it focuses on gross debt, rather than net debt. To the extent that debtors hold assets which they can liquidate in order to service their debt, if needed, gross debt data might overestimate the actual debt burden. But the debt data includes all debt, domestic and foreign. The international investment position reflect assets and liabilities; i.e. net debt. However, it only reflects cross-border assets and liabilities – domestic assets/ liabilities are not reflected – hence the IIP is a reflection of net foreign exposure. Also, the IIP reflects a broader range of assets, some of which are not normally considered debt, such as FDI and equity portfolio; in this sense, the NIIP overestimates the foreign debt. Current status and implementation reality Although the food tax cut remains PM Takaichi’s signature pledge, which she has described as her “long‑cherished wish,” political support has thinned since the start of the year. Takaichi and Ishin remain committed, but parts of the LDP have softened and the DPP has shifted toward cash handouts. At the same time, Keidanren and the NCSS expert advisory committee have argued for skipping bridge measures altogether and accelerating rollout of a basic refundable tax credit. On 8 May, Nikkei Shimbun cited a senior administration source noting that “cash handouts beat tax cuts on speed,” marking the first explicit signal that the Cabinet may be stepping back from the food tax cut. Logistics as the binding constraint The main constraints are implementation and cost. At an NCSS working‑level meeting on 8 April, a METI hearing with major POS vendors indicated that introducing a zero rate on food would require around one year of system changes. records.text: FLASH F L A S H 18/05/2026 1 China: Slower growth in April amid policy headwinds Growth slowdown in April: China’s industrial production growth eased to 4.1% y/y in April, down from 5.7 % in March, while the service output index rose only 4.3 % y/y, slipping from 5.0% previously. The output data suggests that overall economic growth in April likely moderated to about 4.2% y/y, on our estimates, from the robust 5 % y/y increase recorded in Q1. Although we do expect Q2 growth to be slower than Q1, a 4.2% y/y pace is still below our expectation and below this year’s GDP target range of 4.5–5%. Domestic demand the major economic drag: The main culprit behind April’s slowdown was the moderation in domestic demand. Fixed asset investment saw a steep fall of 9.4% y/y in April while retail sales growth moderated to 0.2% y/y in April, the lowest since March 2023. Immediate policy stimulus unlikely: Although April’s growth fell below the lower bound of the GDP target, policymakers are unlikely to roll out fresh stimulus immediately, in our view. The demand-side weakness appears to be policy-driven rather than based on fundamentals. Retail sales were soft because April 2025 benefited from the consumer-goods trade-in subsidies that has been scaled back this year. However, the organic consumption growth was slightly higher in April than the pace recorded in March. Private sector buying JGBs – deposit falls but recovers: Here we try to answer the question whether deposit falls when private sectors shifting money from deposit to JGBs/T-bill (including via MMF). If they do so in the secondary market, total deposit amount should not change, since someone receives the proceed from sale, same as when buying equity in the secondary market. Instead, when new JGBs are funded by private sector, deposit can fall for some time as deposit is withdrawn (Figure 4). However, when the government makes fiscal spending, money shifts back to private sector. Then private sector recovers its deposit. However, the government often overfunds and holds onto the proceed from JGBs for extended time. In the meantime, the deposit does not recover. Such is often the case after Covid as the budget is designed to look large and either takes a form of “fund” or intra-government bill-underwriting. records.text: Chair Jerome Powell expressed a desire to cycle through various forms of bias language in the meeting statement – first to a formal neutral bias, then to a tightening bias – prior to raising rates. If taken literally , this would place the earliest live meeting for a hike in the autumn. Moreover, President Donald Trump has long viewed with suspicion the timing of the 50bp rate cut in September 2024, shortly before the presidential election, and we think a Fed under new leader Kevin Warsh would likely try to avoid repeating this. While markets have gradually been pricing the risk of a rate hike next year, they seem unprepared for a 1999 -style scenario of ‘insurance’ cuts being reversed in succession. We think the options market offers an attractive structure to play for this scenario. Late last week, we bought a SFRH7 a/a+40bp 1x1.5 put spread – a trade that has a maximum payout 40bp above the market ’s current pricing by next March’s Fed meeting. In addition to seeing risks to the US front end, we believe the back end can continue trending higher as well, with the 30y yield having moved decisively above the key 5% level . This is for five reasons: 1) After 30y yields broke the 4% resistance level in 2023, long -end yields de-anchored. Once these measures enter negotiations, they become hard to replace and tend to persist, increasing the likelihood that multiple measures are delivered together. Debate 2: The fiscal framework A second debate is running in parallel over the fiscal framework. The proposed changes include a shift toward multi-year budgeting and the introduction of a dedicated investment envelope, alongside tighter rules on supplementary budgets. Framed as steps to improve fiscal transparency and discipline in an environment of inflation, higher JGB issuance, and rising long‑term spending needs, including defense and industrial policy, these changes also create scope to accommodate higher spending. Where the risk builds Taken together, these two debates point in the same direction. In the household package, measures are more likely to accumulate than replace one another. In the fiscal framework, flexibility is being expanded as spending pressures rise. Policy delivery under PM Takaichi has so far been more restrained than initial market expectations, with periods of rising JGB yields followed by caution. However, these have mainly limited individual measures, while the overall fiscal stance remains expansionary. May signals, June decisions, August test Key signals arrive through the policy calendar. Staying long North Asia (China, Korea, Taiwan) versus vs S Asia (Indonesia, Thailand, India) remains a key FX & equity theme for us partly as global energy stockpiles appear on course for record lows. records.text: sense that deposit falls when individuals buy JGBs After the government makes fiscal spending, the capital should flow through to the private sector, allowing deposits to recover. However, the government often ‘overfunds’ and holds the proceeds for an extended period, preventing quick deposit recovery. This was often the case in Japan. The budget tends to carry a large headline number and takes the form of a ‘fund’ or intra-government bill-underwriting. Government T-bill holdings have risen from zero to about JPY20trn since 2024. The government also parks its cash at the BoJ through a ‘reverse repo’. Figure 5 shows the magnitude of this since 2024. We therefore think such government’s effective cash is another source of declining deposits, even though it is theoretically temporary. There may be cases where deposits are not entirely recovered at all. In Figure 4, we assume that fiscal spending is entirely domestic, so either households or corporations receive the money as (domestic) deposits. But any external spending – such as overseas defence procurement – may prevent domestic banks from recouping those deposits in the same way, or to the same extent, even if funds flow to the banking system in associated transactions. records.text: The increase in markups, and the resulting boost to profit margins, reflects two main forces. First, consumers’ sensitivity to price differences has declined over time, leading them to compare prices less across sellers.6 Economist Hendrik Döpper and co-authors estimate that across more than 100 product categories, US consumers became roughly 30% less price sensitive between 2006 and 2019 (Exhibit 8, left panel). This allowed firms to retain declines in marginal costs as wider profit margins rather than pass them through to consumers. Economist Kunal Sangani attributes lower consumer price sensitivity to rising incomes: higher income raises the opportunity cost of time, leading consumers to search less for lower prices.7 He estimates that increases in average income and in income inequality— which has meant that less price-sensitive households account for a larger share of total consumption—can account for a roughly 8pp rise in the aggregate retail markup from 1980 to 2018 (Exhibit 8, right panel). Consistent with this hypothesis, we find a positive cross-country relationship between the rise in markups and the increase in GDP per capita over 1980-2016 across a sample of advanced economies.8 Second, rising concentration has reduced competition, allowing firms to exert greater market power and charge higher markups. records.text: ab 18 May 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Eurozone: Public debt rising again Eurozone public debt up moderately during 2025 In this report, we look at the latest Eurozone (EZ) debt dynamics (Q4-2025), disaggregated by countries and sectors (governments, households, non-financial corporates, and financial institutions). Relative to GDP , aggregate EZ debt has continued to decline moderately, to 352%. As regards government debt, we need to distinguish between two data sets: According to Eurostat's quarterly financial balance sheet data (EQFBS), public debt-to-GDP fell marginally (-0.2pp) between Q4-24 and Q4-25, to 92%. But public debt according to the methodology used by the EU for monitoring the Stability and Growth Pact (EUSGP) – which is arguably more accurate, more commonly quoted, and more important from a fiscal policy and political perspective – rose by 0.8pp to 87.9% (see Box 1, p. 2). The other sub-sectors saw moderate debt declines. As expected, the tailwinds to public finance consolidation from high GDP deflators (i.e. inflation) – which were very strong in 2022/23 – have moderated, so further debt consolidation will require more policy effort going forward. Although the current energy price shock is now pushing up inflation again, we do not expect much impact on debt dynamics, as GDP deflators are closely correlated with core inflation (not headline), which we expect to rise only modestly. records.text: ab 18 May 2026 Global Research European Equity Strategy Simply Europe: An inflationary slowdown Key takeaways  Positioning for an inflationary slowdown – We are moving our preferences further toward a more stagflation-aware stance as the macro backdrop deteriorates. Growth expectations are weakening (with GDP estimates for 2026 and 2027 now below 2025 levels and economic surprises turning negative), while inflation expectations are rising. After a prolonged recovery/expansion phase since the 2022 energy crisis, both the OECD leading indicators and PMIs are now signalling that Europe is transitioning into an inflationary slowdown regime. This shift requires a more cautious and selective portfolio construction.  Shifting further toward inflation protection and defensives – Our favoured positions reflect a desire for inflation protection (energy, materials) as well as increasing exposure to late-expansion/early-slowdown defensives (utilities, telecoms, pharma). At the same time, we are reducing cyclical risk further (banks move to neutral after years as a most favoured sector). The only cyclicals we still favour are those exposed to structural growth areas (data-centre and AI-linked capex). More recently, the rise of platform markets with strong network effects—where the value of a service grows with its user base, giving early leaders a self-reinforcing advantage—has also contributed to rising concentration. Using detailed industry-level data from the US Economic Census, we estimate that between 2012 and 2022 concentration rose much faster in industries where network effects are stronger. For example, concentration in web search services and in online retail grew roughly five and three times faster than the cross-industry average, respectively. Consistent with the rise of larger, dominant firms, productivity dispersion has also widened following technology shocks. Drawing on the BLS Dispersion Statistics on Productivity, we find that faster technological progress has led to higher subsequent productivity dispersion in manufacturing and retail trade—particularly in technology-producing sectors and in industries most transformed by new technologies, such as online retail (Exhibit 6, left panel). The right panel of Exhibit 6 shows that frontier firms’ productivity growth has far outpaced the economywide average in recent decades. As a result, INR rates have sold off across the curve since the start of the Middle East conflict and continue to be driven by moves in oil prices. Markets are currently pricing in more than 4 rate hikes from the RBI over the next 12 months. While bond demand and supply dynamics suggest that INR rates should be traded with an overall paid bias, we are skeptical about the market's aggressive pricing of rate hikes in the front-end. Inflation (e.g., core CPI excl. precious metals) was relatively low before the conflict, and with fuel prices remaining fixed at the pump, we believe the pass-through to inflation will be slower than expected. Consequently, we think the RBI will not hike rates as much as market pricing and are running a 1s5s steepener in INR NDOIS (see EM rates: Take profit on INR 5y payer, enter 1s5s steepener, dated 11 March). In fact, the increased fiscal costs of maintaining fixed fuel prices will contribute to a widening of the government's fiscal deficit, lending further support to our steepener view.

records.text: 220/05/2026 Battery metals outlook: A balancing act Elena Lee, Commodities Desk Strategist | BNP Paribas London Branch Please ref er to MAR disclosures and important inf ormation at the end of this report KEY MESSAGES Lithium: We raise our lithium forecasts to allow for the effect of persistent supply constraints and bullishness around the demand outlook on market sentiment . We still see the market as fundamentally oversupplied but think a catalyst would be required for sentiment to shift. That might be a reopening of the Jianxiawo mine, or slowdown in energy storage battery production – which we think could occur in late H2 2026. We therefore see downside risks to prices from that point. Cobalt: We maintain a bullish outlook on cobalt prices, anticipating a tighter market in 2026 driven by delayed DRC shipments and possible supply disruptions in Indonesia linked to sulphur shortages. Price upside due to supply tightness and depleting inventories could be capped by weakening EV sales, especially in the US, where ternary batteries dominate . We still see upside risks especially in Q3, when inventories are forecast to reach low levels. An influx of backlogged supply from the DRC during H2 would head this off, but we see this as unlikely given that firms will require time to align with the more complex export procedures in place. Using the regression model’s coefficients, Figure 11 shows the day-by-day evolution of spreads after issuance. We find that the largest tightening occurs between the pricing date (issue spread) and the start of secondary trading. In our sample, the average issue spread is 97.4bp. After issuance, this tightens to 94.7bp, before compressing more gradually to 94.2bp within three and nine business days and 93.5bp after 10 to 60 business days. This pattern reflects the initial new-issue concession: bonds are priced at a discount to attract primary demand, so when they begin trading in the secondary market, this concession is quickly unwound, leading to an immediate tightening in spreads. records.text: 3 Insights SPOTLIGHT CHARTS The dollar’s changing relationships The USD rally and commodity currencies/EM carry sell-off in the immediate aftermath of the Iran conflict’s onset, and the retracement of those moves through April and early May as conditions calm, speak to a recoupling of FX trends with risk markets not seen in a while. After briefly shedding the persistently negative correlation to US equities that prevailed between 2020 and 2024 last year, the US dollar has spent most of 2026 winning its safe haven credentials back. USD skew showing no bias As notably, the USD’s positive correlation to implied FX volatility is as strong as it has been at any point in the last five years. Unlike what we have seen recently in equities (more below) where a weaker spot-vol relationship briefly emerged, leading to expected lesser demand for downside, the FX implications are clearer. The USD’s strong positive correlation to volatility may not last. But if it does, USD call skew looks very underpriced given the lack of bias in either short- or long-dated risk reversals. Are equity markets too frothy? Equity market price action has had an increasingly grabby feel to it, made manifest in the less negative correlation between spot and volatility markets at an index level. Accordingly, the Eurozone IIP shows the outstanding amount and composition of EZ residents’ financial claims on non-residents and EZ residents’ financial liabilities to non-residents. The difference between assets and liabilities is the net international investment position (NIIP) and represents either a net claim on, or a net liability to, non-Eurozone residents. The IIP is valued on the basis of prevailing market prices and exchange rates at the end of each period. Changes in the IIP are a function of: (a) transactions, (b) revaluations (i.e. changes in asset prices / exchange rates) and (c) other volume changes (i.e. reclassifications, write- downs, changes in sources/methods, or changes in the residency of companies). records.text: tten. The current global environment, marked by geopolitical tensions such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, is likely to keep foreign investors' appetite for IndoGBs subdued. Indeed, we see limited foreigner net inflows for Indonesian government securities in 2026, following large outflows towards the end of 2025 as markets increasingly converged on the view that BI may not be able to deliver further rate cuts (Figure 9). This subdued outlook has persisted into 2026, despite growing AUMs of EM funds, suggesting fund managers remain underweight IndoGBs. Indonesia's budget deficit, which reached 2.92% of GDP in 2025, is close to the government's 3% ceiling. While the government has pledged to keep the deficit below 3%, fiscal concerns may continue to weigh on investors’ minds, particularly in the back end. This will likely remain a concern on investors in 2026, as elevated oil prices may exacerbate the fiscal burden on the government, as Indonesia's significant petrol subsidies will become increasingly costly if oil prices remain high for an extended period. The introduction of Bank Indonesia Rupiah Securities (SRBI) in the second half of 2023 has had a notable impact on the market. Although SRBI has attracted foreign inflows due to its attractive carry, it has failed to support the IDR, as most of these foreign flows are FX-hedged. Hence, we don’t expect a significant increase in rates. We believe China’s ‘slow bull’ equity market is likely to lead to a very gradual reallocation of investments from fixed income into the equity market. The PBoC’s latest report estimated that 80% of asset managers’ investments were in fixed income, of which half were interbank deposits or negotiable certificates of deposit. That said, with low yields from deposits, retail investors are increasingly interested in ‘fixed income+’ investment strategies that include some allocation to riskier assets, such as equities. On each given day, we blend data by adding the total quoted amount in the order book from both sources for each displayed currency pair. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. For example, a 90th percentile reading for EURUSD indicates that the current depth of book value is ranked in the top 10% of historical observations over the last year. Volume data from July 2020 onwards represents the combined total traded volume across EBS and Reuters sources. Prior to July 2020, we aggregate total traded volume from EBS with estimated trading volume from Reuters, which is calculated as a product of total paid-given count and average trade size. To estimate average trade size prior to July 2020 we use all future data for total trading volume and trade count. We then apply a 20-day moving average and rank the current value over the prior one-year lookback window**. Spread data represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. A budget framework built for a deflationary environment tightens in real terms once inflation returns, adding to pressure for ad hoc fiscal measures. At the same time, structural spending commitments with delayed or uncertain payoffs are rising, including defense, industrial policy, and social security. These pressures are difficult to reconcile with a framework still geared toward short‑term control rather than multi‑year prioritization. The macro backdrop has also shifted. Our dealer balance sheet capacity utilization proxy has fallen by 10% since the middle of March and remains well below highs seen during Liberation Day (Figure 5). Lower RMP pace is likely temporary RMP reduction likely temporary: Our base case remains for the Fed to maintain RMPs close to $25bn/month. The timing and sizing of future RMPs seem to be at the New York Fed’s discretion. The timing of the first step down from $40bn/month to $25bn/month in April was largely anticipated, but the pace and size were not. Since then, the Fed has not indicated any further reductions would be needed and yet it has reduced the pace by another $15bn, to $10bn/month. We understand that recent softness in repo pushed the second reduction in RMPs to $10bn/month, but we see this as temporary. We do not expect this reduction to last beyond Q3 as July-August and October-November tend to be negative for funding dynamics due to both high Treasury issuance and elevated TGA balances (Figure 6). Since February 2022, the RBA has ceased making new bond purchases and has instead adopted a passive approach, allowing the existing bonds on its balance sheet to mature without replacement. This approach has resulted in a reduction of the RBA's bond holdings, contributing to an increase in net bond supply to the market over the years. Notably, net market supply has tended to be much larger in Q1 and Q3 than Q2 and Q4 due to the maturity schedule of ACGBs (which is focused on Q2 and Q4). In contrast, bond syndications have occurred in Q1 and Q3 over the past few years, exacerbating the seasonality. For the remainder of FY25/26, we estimate a weekly bond supply of about AUD2bn. The AOFM debt management office is set to conduct a 10y Green Treasury Bond syndication in the second half of FY25/26. We estimate the size at around AUD7bn, using the previous Green Bond syndication as a gauge. Two more tankers were loaded with ~2.6 mb of crude but their destination is currently unknown. - For the week-ending May 17th, daily crude exports averaged 3.7 mb/d with another ~0.4 mb/d of loadings for which destination is currently unknown. - Saudi Arabia's target of maximum throughput on its 7 mb/d East-West pipeline (full capacity) will require Yanbu port to sustainably deliver 5 mb/d of crude and oil products exports (2 mb/d is domestic consumption). For context, Saudi Arabia was exporting ~ 7 mb/d of oil pre- war of which only ~ 1mb/d had been routed via Yanbu. - Risk of disruption to this supply route from Iran and its proxies remain meaningful, especially attacks by the Houthis on tankers transiting the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait. A senior Iranian official had hinted last month that Iran might retaliate to the US blockade on the Strait of Hormuz by attacking Saudi Arabia’s exports along the Bab-el- Mandeb Strait. records.text: Deutsche Bank. Research 5 The U.S. Blockade in practice The US claims the blockade has redirected 81 Iran-linked vessels. More than 12 US ships are reportedly involved, with 100+ fighter and surveillance aircraft. As part of the blockade, the US has seized Iran-linked vessels. - The US has stated its blockade of Iranian ships will continue until negotiations occur and an agreement to end the war is reached; however, if the basis for a peace deal is agreed, reports suggest that restrictions may gradually be lifted. - So far under the blockade, the US has seized at least 3 Iranian vessels, with two being detained away from the Middle-East region (in the Indian Ocean). Iran has responded with its own seizures of ships in the Strait of Hormuz. - The blockade officially entered force on April 13 at 10am ET and applies to “vessels of all nations entering or departing Iranian ports and coastal areas” (though an exemption exists for humanitarian ships). In its initial implementation, the blockade focused on the Gulf of Oman, rather than in the Persian Gulf or Strait of Hormuz itself (see map below). The blockade does not apply to non-Iran linked ships, however President Trump had also previously stated that vessels who have paid tolls to Iran would also be targeted by the US Navy. UK 10y not a buy yet - Receiving June 'BoE We have been telling clients not to go long UK 10y bonds as we think that political risks had been underpriced. Clients have been asking how much gilt yields could reprice in response to political developments. As a reference point, we estimate that around 90bps of additional term premium was priced into 10-year gilts in 2022 following Liz Truss’s mini-budget. Although baseline forecasts do not include Fed hikes this year, risks of a hawkish pivot have risen. We outline scenarios that could force an FOMC response and the indicators to watch. • With commodity price pressures rising amid the Strait of Hormuz blockage and AI-related capex straining parts of the global supply chain, risks of a hawkish Fed turn have clearly intensified. While consensus economist baselines do not include hikes, markets have taken notice, with pricing for a hike by December 2026 now exceeding 60%. • Although our baseline also does not anticipate hikes through end-2027, we agree that upside risks to the policy rate have intensified. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 3 EV slowdown may weigh on demand: Despite market exuberance over demand for lithium from Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), we prefer to focus on electric vehicles (EVs), given that they still account for over 60% of lithium demand . As laid out in Electric vehicles : Crisis to catalyst, dated 14 May, China Q1 passenger EV sales were weaker than expected as the world’s largest EV market transitions towards maturity, with lower tax benefits, tighter eligibility requirements for subsidies and stricter anti-involution rules. Lacklustre sales in the US and China offset strength in the EU, and global passenger EV sales were up just 3% y/y in Q1 – if we zoom in on BEV and PHEV sales alone, global sales were down 1% y/y. While we expect EV penetration to rise globally for the rest of the year as the Middle East conflict incentivises electrification away from oil dependence, absolute EV sales may still suffer if the risks to economic growth prompt a standstill in the auto industry. We therefore expect global passenger EV sales growth of just 17% in 2026, almost half that of 2025, and 17% again in 2027 as a balance is struck between the lingering economic impact of the Middle East conflict and that stronger electrification push. records.text: ector parties (such as households/corporates) via the same mechanism as private non-bank purchases (Figure 6, below). The difference between Figure 4 and 6 is whether there is an initial outflow from deposit or not. When banks buy JGBs, there is no deposit outflow, so deposits only increases in net terms as fiscal spending is done. Of course, the government may be slow to carry out such spending as we discussed above. Based on the factors discussed previously for BoJ QT and private non-bank bond buying, we can summarize that deposits increase in net terms when either the BoJ or banks buy JGBs (i.e., extend credit). Conversely, deposits fall when reverse takes place. We simply go back to the banking principle of deposit creation. As shown in the right side of Figure 6, deposit is created when banks lend to the private sector. The difference is that credit to the private sector creates deposits instantly, while lending to the government introduces a lag. Between 2022 and 2024, banks trimmed JGB holdings anticipating higher interest rates, while the BoJ kept buying JGBs under its YCC (yield curve control) policy. But after 2024, the BoJ cut JGB holdings, while banks increased some (Figure 7, above). Therefore, the reduction of deposits due to the BoJ’s QT since 2024 was partly offset in net terms by banks buying JGBs. The range of proposals makes it difficult to form a coherent view of where policy is heading. In practice, the picture is evidently simpler. Most of the noise reflects two parallel tracks: household transfers and the fiscal framework. Debate 1: Household transfers and the bridges The first debate, and the one driving most of the news flow, concerns structural reform of household income transfers. The endpoint is a refundable tax credit targeting middle-to-low income workers. But implementation will take time and requires cross-party support. records.text: M Idea 4 Bond RV. The current CTD, 1E 39, has richened recently in spot terms. This is visible both in outright ASW valuations and in the closest-neighbour ASW fly shown in Exhibit 4 . Because both contracts share the same CTD and CTD-switch risk is negligible, outright CTD richness should largely affect M6 and U6 symmetrically. A more important roll channel is therefore relative funding and repo specialness across the front and back delivery periods. Repo considerations. The 1E 39 trades approximately 20bp rich versus SONIA in repo for the front contract, while trading broadly flat versus SONIA for the back contract, using mid-market repo levels. If front-contract repo richness fades relative to the back contract, M6 fair value should rise relative to U6, driving the roll richer. Conversely, if front-contract repo richens further relative to the back contract, the roll should cheapen. Exhibit 5 shows the roll’s sensitivity to a parallel shift in term repo rates. Under this parallel-shift assumption, lower term repo would richen the roll, while higher term repo would cheapen it, all else equal. Central bank pricing. The June MPC meeting on 18-Jun-2026 could also be a key driver of roll valuations through its impact on market pricing. At the time of writing, ~8bp of hikes are priced in, while our baseline case is for the BoE to remain on hold. If market pricing converges toward our base case, term repo should move lower and the M6/U6 roll should richen, as shown in Exhibit 5 .

records.text: market rates having trended lower in the last few months. The new $10bn pace is below our steady-state pace of $25bn/month, highlighting that the timing and sizing of future RMP adjustments are at the discretion of the NY Fed’ SOMA desk, as it adapts to a fluid money market environment. We expect this $10bn pace to be temporary and see the Fed raising the pace again by Q4, back to our steady state estimate of $25bn. Ever since QT ended in December (Figure 1), money market rates have trended lower. More recently, repo has settled well below IORB over the last month. We largely attribute this to the Fed opting for an overly aggressive RMP pace earlier this year, alongside negative T-bill issuance over the past month. Additional tailwinds such as (1) a sharp rise in MMF assets, (2) dealer balance sheet relief, and the (3) Fed's campaign to lower reserve demand – are likely amplifying the softness in repo. The SOFR/FF curve – from August to December - sits near our estimated equilibrium range of -2bp and -4bp. Pricing for the next few months is likely to remain soft, but we look to fade any move in SOFR/FF above -2bp in forward contracts after July. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear Structural fall in bond demand: Historically, banks and insurers have been the main purchasers of government securities (Figure 5). However, insurance industry growth has slowed to around 6% y/y and banks' demand for bonds has fallen due to a pickup in credit growth and regulatory changes limiting transfers to and from their held-to-maturity books. Meanwhile, the Employees' Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), India’s pension and social security body, is shifting away from fixed income and towards equities as it seeks to boost returns. Foreign investor ownership of IGBs also remains low, accounting for only 3% of outstanding bonds. We expect this to continue, as the rate-cutting cycle is over, and high taxes and FX-hedging costs limit the potential returns for foreign participants. Steepener bias on INR rates: The current high oil price environment poses a significant challenge for India, one of the largest oil importers in Asia. As a result, INR rates have sold off across the curve since the start of the Middle East conflict and continue to be driven by moves in oil prices. Markets are currently pricing in almost four rate hikes from the RBI over the next 12 months. While bond demand and supply dynamics suggest INR rates should be traded with an overall paid bias, we are skeptical about the market's pricing of aggressive rate hikes in the front-end. We think that the MAS is likely to continue focusing its FX policy on mitigating upside risks to inflation, as it is currently driven by external factors. This is evident in the MAS's decision to increase the SGDNEER slope at its April meeting. Given the persistence of high oil prices, there is a risk of further tightening at subsequent meetings, which is why we remain long SGDNEER (see FX: Long SGDNEER ahead of April MAS meeting, dated 17 March). On the other hand, the reduction in global energy supplies poses downside risks to growth, particularly since Singapore's economy is heavily reliant on regional and global trade. To counter this, we expect the MAS to maintain accommodative monetary conditions by keeping liquidity levels flush, which will help keep front-end SORA rates low. Additionally, we think safe-haven-seeking flows into Singapore are likely to continue, further contributing to the abundance of liquidity (Figure 5). In contrast, the belly and back end of SORA rates have a higher sensitivity to global rates. Together, they allow more near‑term spending without it appearing in headline fiscal metrics. The experience with trust funds (基金) shows how this can develop in practice. records.text: European Economic Perspectives18 May 2026 ab 2 Box 1: Eurozone government debt – two definitions To calculate outstanding debt by sector (governments, households, non-financial corporates, and financial institutions), we predominantly use Eurostat's quarterly financial balance sheet data (EQFBS), specifically loans and debt securities. As regards the public sector, these calculations suggest that in Q4-25 Eurozone government debt amounted to 92% of GDP (essentially unchanged from 92.2% in Q4-24). This is above the 87.9% (+0.8pp from Q4-24) reported by Eurostat's quarterly government debt data (EUSGP), which follows the European System of Accounts (ESA 2010) and is the basis for the EU's Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP). EQFBS and EUSGP differ mainly for two reasons: 1. Government debt for EDP purposes (EUSGP) is recorded at nominal value while financial balance sheet data (EQFBS) is recorded at market prices; this can create a discrepancy between the two measures when market interest rates, and hence bond prices, are subject to significant change. 2. Government debt for EDP purposes (EUSGP) is consolidated between and within the sectors of general government, while financial balance sheet data (EQFBS) is unconsolidated and might therefore lead to some double-counting, as debt between government sectors might not be netted out. For this reason, we regard the debt data for EDP purposes (EUSGP) as the more accurate measure; it is also the more important measure from a political

records.text: [26Y est.] SX7P, 2026 EPS expectations Implied December 2026 ECB rate Source: UBS, Bloomberg Earnings: Banks generate earnings primarily through the deposit beta but also from releases of provisions for non-performing loans (as the cycle improves) and more recently, effective cost control/cutting into the expansion. Investors often say 'the ECB is about to hike' which may improve profitability for banks. However, the chart below shows that consensus EPS estimates have been tracking the market-implied ECB rate recently. The hikes might already be in earnings expectations leaving further upward revisions hard to come by. As growth slows, it is possible banks will need to start raising their provisions for non-performing loans. And finally, effective cost control seemed to be a driver of EPS revisions for the last several years but positive surprises on cost-control have abated in the last three earnings periods. Valuations: Structurally, European banks remain very cheap. Cyclically, valuations are often more sensitive to the level of bond yields and the slope of the bond curve. With inflation expectations pushing bond yields higher recently, bank valuations have been supported (and defensives valuations hurt). If inflation expectations begin to peak and we start to see more concerns about slower growth, bond yields may peak and possibly reverse. Debt data and the IIP offer different perspectives; we see them as complements, not substitutes, in identifying potential vulnerabilities from high debt. The debt data covers both domestic and foreign debt, but it leaves out assets, i.e. it reflects gross debt, not net debt. The IIP reflects assets and liabilities, but only on a cross-border basis, i.e. it leaves out domestic assets/liabilities. Also, the IIP includes a broader range of assets, some of which are not normally considered debt, such as FDI or equity portfolio. A number of EZ countries have high aggregate debt, but a positive NIIP – e.g. Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Belgium or Finland. And what's happening with deficits? A quick look at the EU's EDP procedures Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, Malta and Slovakia (as well as the non- EZ countries Hungary, Poland and Romania) are currently in an Excessive Deficit Procedure (EDP). Of those countries, Malta reduced its deficit to below 3% of GDP in 2025, suggesting that it might exit the EDP when EU Finance Ministers discuss the matter in June. Italy's deficit remained slightly above 3% in 2025, making it uncertain whether it can exit the EDP this year, even though it plans to reduce the deficit in 2026. While AFPs could unwind non-hedging FX derivatives to meet the LED requirement if needed, it is unclear how much the overall FX-derivative portfolio would actually change. AFPs may still expand hedging activity, and the liquidity-ratio requirement could also affect these positions—a factor that is difficult to assess because detailed public data are unavailable. AFPs’ FX activity takes a back seat in USDCLP and the cross-currency basis: In the short run we expect AFPs’ activity to have only a modest effect on the CLP exchange rate and on the CLP basis. Over the medium term, however, a larger amount of FX hedging by AFPs could push USDCLP lower and compress the CLP basis. Since AFPs own a large share of foreign assets, their hedging choices affect not only the CLP but also the cross-currency basis (see CLP: Further underperformance likely in medium term, 24 February 2024). An increase in the AFP hedging ratio would support the CLP, lower FX points and compress the CLP basis (see Chile: Pension fund hedging shift to stabilize CLP basis, 17 September). Prices, however, appear to have derailed from fundamentals – and will likely continue to do so in the near term, due to the factors we set out on earlier pages . At this point, we think a catalyst is required to spark a shift in market sentiment that allows prices to more readily reflect fundamentals . This could arrive in H2 2026, if the Jianxiawo mine restarts as we expect, if more details are released on Zimbabwe export quotas or if there is a decisive move towards de-escalation in the Middle East . In any case, overproduction is unsustainable in the long run and inventories built up will eventually have to be deployed. This can only occur if production slows or deployment speeds up to match or outpace production. We see the latter as less likely due to infrastructure constraints, with downside risks to prices should producers ease off in the face of storage concerns or fading sentiment . It is an open question how much inventory the supply chain can handle, so we watch for any slowdown in production or sales. records.text: M Idea 6 Last week, we published our Mid-Year outlook. For those looking for the 2-minute version: We’re took our forward 12-month (mid-2027) price target up to 8300. That’s 20.5x forward EPS of $404. Our year-end 2026 price target moved up from 7800 to 8000. The main messages here are: 1. This is an earnings story, not a multiple expansion one. 2. This outlook builds on three themes we have emphasized since last year: running the economy/earnings cycle hot, public to private rebalancing, and a broadening of earnings and performance. 3. The fear of AI is leading many companies to "run it lean" in an economy that is also running hot. This has only boosted the operating leverage and margins further and one reason we raised our EPS forecasts last week. In our baseline, we have 2026 EPS of $339 (23% growth), 2027 EPS of $380 (12% growth), and 2028 EPS of $429 (13% growth). The drivers of our resilient earnings forecast are: positive operating leverage and margin expansion aided by AI adoption, stabilizing pricing power in goods oriented end markets and a capex cycle that continues to show momentum. The higher frequency earnings data is supportive of our view and this is clearly the strongest earnings backdrop we’ve seen since 2021. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear 1718/05/2026 Gross and net supply: Overall, gross and net supply for government bonds in FY26 is expected to be in line with FY25, which included two supplementary budgets. Gross issuance for FY26 is expected to total KRW225.7trn (Figure 1), while net supply is expected to be KRW108.4trn (Figure 3). Bond supply unaffected by supplementary budget this year: In recent years, South Korea has tended to come up with supplementary budgets, and fiscal spending has increased significantly under the government of President Lee Jae-myung. Most recently, the Ministry of Planning and Budget has proposed a supplementary budget of KRW26.2trn, but this will not result in any additional bond issuance and will be funded through surplus tax revenues from an outperforming semiconductor industry. In fact, the government aims to repay KRW1trn of outstanding debt in an effort to reduce the pressure on bond markets. Seasonal trends: The Ministry of Economy and Finance tends to slightly front-load its annual borrowing plans in H1, with bond issuance typically tailing off towards the end of the year (Figure 2). For FY2026, issuance in H1 is expected to account for around 55–60% of annual supply. In terms of bond maturities, Korea Treasury Bonds (KTB) tend to mature at the end of every quarter (March, June, September, December), leading to a dip in net bond supply in those months (Figure 4). Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Research The index performs well after months of heavy issuance Index extension remains a powerful and predictable technical driver of near-term IG performance. The indices to which investors are benchmarked rebalance monthly. Since index duration jumps on the rebalancing date as newly issued bonds enter and <1y bonds roll out, benchmarked investors are forced to buy duration to avoid tracking error. Large index extensions, like in March this year, are typically due to a rush of issuance with a healthy mix of long-dated supply. The index tends to tighten significantly following a large extension month. From t-20 to month-end (a proxy for the full trading month) for months we identify as having a meaningfully elevated extension3 , the median move for index spreads is 3bp tighter, but not in a straight path. Historically, spreads widen marginally in the first half of the month before tightening meaningfully as the supply headwind wanes, and this technical tends to continue throughout the following month, with a further 6-7bp of tightening (Figure 12). The same holds true when excluding COVID-affected months (Figure 13). The tightening is realised only when the extension is noticeably elevated. records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 20/05/2026 1 Surging use of derivatives by Chilean pension funds (AFPs) over recent years has fundamentally reshaped their risk profiles, prompting the local regulator to issue guidance laying out procedures and deadlines that AFPs must meet to regularize their derivative holdings. In turn, this may prompt broad portfolio rebalancing. Because AFPs have substantial exposure to local rate (Camara) curves and their FX derivative positions play a key role in driving USDCLP and the CLP cross-currency basis, we elaborate below on these exposures and their possible market implications. Specifically, two key risk-mitigation metrics are being introduced: 1. LED (Maximum Derivative Exposure Limit): Defined as the estimated loss of a fund’s derivative portfolio under stressed market conditions, expressed as a percentage of the fund’s total assets. 2. RCL (Liquidity Coverage Ratio): Defined as the amount of liquid assets available (by currency group) divided by the potential liquidity demand created by derivative operations in that currency group. AFPs have a 210-day window (which began on 9 April) to satisfy both requirements. First, the projected loss on an AFP’s derivatives portfolio must stay below a ceiling of roughly 2-3% based on the fund type. Second, each AFP must maintain enough liquid assets to cover any collateral calls that its derivatives could trigger (Figure 1). Underlying weakness in the K-shaped economy was revealed further as policy momentum faded. The Mideast conflict and elevated energy prices also played a role in April, and could create a further layer in the divergent economy. Upstream price and profitability improvements have not translated into investment or capex amid supply shocks, while downstream sectors saw a further demand hit, as shown in April’s data. Headline numbers especially nominal readings could still be solid, yet stagflation risks are rising. We expect policy actions to start now with fiscal implementation. To be sure, recent productivity data would argue against this risk: Nonfarm business productivity rose nearly 3% over the four quarters to Q1 26, roughly twice the pre-pandemic pace. However, the San Francisco Fed's utilization-adjusted measures suggest these gains may be overstated, plausibly by about 1.5pp, pointing to a softer underlying supply backdrop than headline figures imply. Recent FOMC discussions have brought these dynamics into sharper focus. In remarks on May 8, Chicago Fed President Goolsbee highlighted the risk that expectations of persistently stronger productivity could pull forward demand, putting upward pressure on the neutral rate. On this view, the near-term macro effects of AI may be more demand-accelerating than disinflationary —contrasting with the prevailing Greenspan-era narrative that technology-led efficiency gains will primarily ease inflation. The key distinction is that in the current episode, prospective productivity gains are already widely anticipated by markets and, therefore, reflected in financial conditions and spending behavior. By contrast, the Greenspan-era experience was characterized by productivity gains that were not easily recognized, allowing supply to improve without an immediate demand response. Given the complexity of the estimation, we believe our approach helps provide a sense on the magnitude of change. Competition for deposits and the perception of shortage: Although total deposits are determined by the factors we discussed – credit extension and fiscal spending, a perceived deposit shortage persists. We think that one factor for such sense is banks competing for deposits. For example, when a bank creates deposits by lending to a corporation, the funds may be transferred to another bank for payment for some purchase, forcing the original bank to win the deposit back. We can compare this to the JGB market: JGB supply is fixed; if demand wanes, prices fall until equilibrium is reached. Deposit pricing mechanism is much slower and not always done not by price but ancillary services. Therefore, the deposit competition is more complex. Another factor behind the perceived shortage is that retail deposits have grown less than corporate deposits. As in Figure 9, both segments rose similarly in absolute terms since 2022, but retail deposits increased 10% versus 15% for corporates, because the retail base is far larger. Under the NSFR (net stable funding requirement) regulation, retail deposits count 90–95% toward stable funding, compared with only 50% for corporate deposits. 418/05/2026 Competition adds to the perception

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Thoughts from the Road We spent the last week on the road meeting with investors and discussing our recently published mid-year outlook. Conversations centered around AI, Iran war impacts and a potential broadening of market leadership. In terms of AI, the discussion was focused on the capex cycle that appears to have taken another step function higher around the accelerated use of agents and the revenue being generated by the model companies. We didn’t hear much concern around the capex momentum stalling, but there is some growing anxiety related to the stock performance in the areas benefitting the most—i.e., memory and other semiconductor stocks. Interestingly, that anxiety stems more from a lack of exposure rather than too much. No investor we spoke with thought that these stocks are shorts, but given the move to date, some were of the view that they could see a healthy correction simply given the extreme crowding and price momentum witnessed in the space. For the hyperscalers, the mood is more mixed and in line with the stock performance—i.e., GOOGL and AMZN preferred on a relative basis. We turned positive on the hyperscalers at the beginning of April given the cheap valuation and strong earnings trends. Despite recent outperformance, the stocks still appear cheap relative to growth.
