Over the course of the trip, we spoke with roughly three dozen clients across hedge funds, asset managers, and banks. Several key themes from these discussions were notable. Strong consensus for bearish bond bias: It was likely in part a function of the price action during the week of our trip, but there was a strong bearish bond bias across clients. As an example, at a breakfast with ~12 clients, all but one leaned bearish bonds. Most of the questions on the US front-end focused on what could get the Fed to hike, and conditional on hiking, how high rates could go. While some saw the potential for the Fed to deliver "insurance hikes" this year – i.e., earlier hikes of a smaller magnitude – most saw it lagging the data, supporting higher term premia out the curve. AJ Rice on HCA Healthcare: We see HCA as a core holding that allows investors to participate in the secular growth of utilization in the healthcare services segment. As the leading operator in the space with a strong hospital and outpatient portfolio, HCA should continue to deliver favorable results over 2026 and beyond. The company has a long history of navigating well in an changing/uncertain environment and should benefit next year from a bolus of capital projects coming online, new payer contracts in key markets and $6-8 bln in annual share repurchases. We also believe HCA may be one of the largest AI winners, as use cases to drive efficiencies across the hospital business are numerous. Kevin Caliendo on CVS Health Corp: We see opportunity for material near-to-mid term earnings improvement for CVS, as the company re-prices multiple underperforming books of business today within the healthcare benefits segment (Aetna), and addresses the operating losses within Oak Street for 2026.

This group earns too much to qualify for existing welfare programs, but not enough to absorb the steady rise in social insurance contributions and consumption taxes alongside weak real wage growth. This diagnosis is broadly shared across the LDP’s technocratic wing, the Ministry of Finance, the DPP, other centrist parties, and the expert advisory committee under the non-partisan National Council for Social Security (NCSS), the multi-party body established in February 2026 to negotiate the package. Across these groups, there is broad recognition that middle-to-low income workers are poorly served by the current system. Conventional tax cuts deliver the same per yen benefit to high earners as to this cohort. Existing welfare programs, meanwhile, are designed for households further down the income distribution. A refundable tax credit fills this gap by providing support even when the credit exceeds income tax owed. The fight is over the bridges Although the endpoint of a refundable tax credit is not in question, the political contest is over the “bridges” needed to reach it. While consensus around the refundable tax credit is strong, implementation will take time: around two years for a simplified national delivery system, and several more for a full rollout incorporating individuals’ financial assets. This mechanism is the main reason why in recent years we often have an intra- year mini cycle, with strong 1Q, weaker 2Q, then policy turns sometime in 3Q, then 4Q rebounds. Market forecasts on annual growth tends to go up after 1Q data releases, go down after 2Q releases and then go back up towards the end of the year. Whether we see a repeat of this remains a question. An immediate adjustment to the tightening overshooting is needed. One good thing compared to earlier years is the PBOC has been keeping liquidity conditions very loose since April, in light of weak credit growth. The magnitude and breath of April slowdown is so significant that we expect administrative policy to respond without the need to wait for the next senior level regular policy meeting. The difficulty with this kind of policy change is it is hard to gauge and impossible to quantify an ante. Even with a reversal in policy stance, weakness in April suggests Q2 GDP growth is likely under pressure. Data anomalies will likely pose additional difficulties as it was the case with FAI data in 2H2025. In general, data under GDP accounting (e.g. Gross Capital Formation under GDP instead of Fixed Asset Investment Completed; Consumption under GDP instead of Retail Sales), foreign trade, and money and credit are of relatively higher quality. Since then, the 5y yield has breached 3% many times, and the box has remained relatively range-bound (Figure 3), making us more confident in entering the trade now. Even if the curve fails to flatten, we find its positive carry quite appealing (0.4bp/m). The 5s30s SPGB–GER box typically flattens when country spreads tighten (Figure 4). A de-escalation in geopolitical tensions could provide a catalyst for the box to move lower. Moreover, we think the medium-term economic fundamentals for Spain remain supportive for extending the flattening of the credit curve, all else equal. Alternative trade structures, such as a 5s10s SPGB–GER flattener, also look attractive but offer flat/negative carry. We note the richness of the 5y sector is evident in the SPGB 3s5s10s fly (Figure 5), and against the PGB curve (Figure 6) as well. KEY MESSAGES The 5y SPGB–Bund spread trades 5bp tighter than before the Middle East conflict began. We think outright buying in the 5y SPGB could have contributed to the tightening. We enter a 5s30s SPGB–GER flattener to fade the richness of the 5y sector. The stabilisation of the curve in the recent sell-off makes us more confident to enter now. How to track the negotiations Negotiations over the design of the refundable tax credit system and the “bridges” to get there are centered on the NCSS. The Council is expected to release an interim report by “early summer,” most likely within June. The Council operates on three tiers: a plenary session, a working‑level committee, and an expert advisory committee. Investors should focus on the working‑level committee, where most of the substantive work is taking place. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: POLICY POSSIBILITIES, DIALING DOLLARS TO NEUTRAL USD selling continues. There can be no doubting the current behavioural set up for the US dollar: institutional investors are heavily underweight, but continue to sell with a degree of strength rarely seen (Figure 1, page 1). Taking a shorter-term perspective, the selling over the last five days looks even stronger. Broader risk-taking, of which USD selling is a crucial part, remains oriented to the positive, with our Behavioural Risk Scorecard positive since early April, after showing only shallow risk reduction in the month following the opening of the Iran conflict and closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But we move neutral. So it was not without significant debate that we close our two USD shorts this week, against NZD and NOK. Ongoing rate market volatility weighs heavily in our decision, as does the broader pricing for potential USD outcomes in FX option markets. Last week, in our Volatility Current piece, we highlighted the value of USD call options, predicated on a renewed negative correlation between the USD and equities, a positive correlation between the USD and FX volatility, the frothiness in equity markets perhaps warranting a short-term pull-back in risk and the lack of any skew for USD options in spite of these factors. The problem here is that the economics team highlight that a lot of these savings have been transferred to more illiquid assets (see here). We also feel that savings ratios tend to fall when real estate prices rise and interest rates are low. Rates are expected to rise 50bp in EZ and while house prices are up 3.5% YoY in Europe, the rise in mortgage rates will likely impact the housing market negatively (with two thirds of mortgages being long dated and a one third being floating). The other offset would be government financial support to the household. In the aftermath of the Ukraine crisis, this amounted to 1.8% of GDP in 2022 and 1.3% of GDP in 2023. The problem is now that the fiscal positions are worse, bond yields are rising and so far the government support to households has been just 0.1% of GDP (though it might rise to c0.5% of GDP according to UBS). records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear Gross supply to rise: We expect Indonesia's gross bond supply to rise in 2026, extending the upward trend seen since 2024. For this analysis, we focus on tradable bonds, which include IndoGBs and sukuk with both fixed and variable rates. We estimate the gross supply of these bonds to reach IDR973trn in 2026, up from IDR837trn in 2025 (Figure 2). Although we expect the net supply of these tradable bonds to decrease from last year's levels, overall net supply may remain elevated due to an increase in other types of bonds, such as retail bonds, private placements and foreign-currency bonds. Seasonally, April tends to see a decrease in bond supply, primarily due to fewer auctions. This year, we think the decline in net supply was probably more pronounced, as there were significant bond maturities in April. Additionally, Bank Indonesia has been actively supporting the bond market over the past two years by increasing its holdings of IndoGBs via auctions and secondary-market purchases, absorbing a significant portion of the supply (Figure 1). Looking ahead, we expect BI to continue its support in helping to stabilize the bond market. Buyers/holders of IndoGBs and sukuk: The share of foreign ownership in outstanding bonds has been declining, while domestic investors, particularly insurance companies and individual holders, have been increasing their holdings (Figure 8, overleaf). records.text: ofit on the Mbonos ASW tightener We are taking profit on our 2038 Mbonos-10y TIIE-F asset swap receiver position, as the spread has moved in our favor, booking a gain of xxbp (USDxxk). The asset-swap spread tightened as Banxico closing its easing cycle at its most recent monetary-policy meeting, opening the door for Mbonos outperformance amid a strengthening peso. Meanwhile, in recent sessions the spread has continued to demonstrate its positive asymmetry—its reaction to tightening forces is much stronger, while widening pressure remains relatively muted. Nevertheless, the ongoing uncertainty in the Middle East—especially the risk that peace talks could progress rapidly— prompted us to lock in profits now. We will wait for a better entry opportunity, as the spread still appears to have room to tighten further. To recap, we initiated the position on 27 April, arguing that external uncertainty creates an asymmetric risk that favours a tightening of the wide spread. The trade is also supported by the prospect of increased foreign ownership of Mbonos, underpinned by Mexico’s stable political environment, a robust MXN, and modest fiscal pressures (see EM rates: Entering 2038 Mbonos ASW receiver).

records.text: of the 21 Eurozone countries project rising deficits in 2026, nine countries expect lower deficits and one country (Austria) an unchanged deficit. ...with a large increase in Germany The largest deficit increases in 2026 are planned in Germany (+1.6pp to 4.3%) and Estonia (+2.3pp to 4.3%). Deficit declines are planned in countries that are in Excessive Deficit Procedures (EDP), including Italy (-0.2pp to 2.9%) and France (-0.1pp to 5%), as well as in Spain (-0.3pp to 2.1%). While we expect Malta to exit the EDP this year (based on a lower deficit in 2025), the decision about Italy is more uncertain, given that its 2025 deficit, at 3.1% of GDP , remained slightly above the 3% mark. Without the increase in the German deficit, the Eurozone deficit would remain unchanged in 2026 at 2.9%. The Eurozone government debt ratio is set to rise from 87.8% of GDP in 2025 to 91.3% in 2026, according to the annual progress reports. Fiscal easing in 2026 of around 0.2% of GDP from national budgets Looking at the Eurozone fiscal impulse in 2026, measured by the change in the cyclically adjusted primary balance (CAPB), suggests moderate easing of 0.2% of GDP in 2026, the first time since 2021 (Figure 5E u r o z o n e , c h a n g e i n c y c l i c a l l y a d j u s t e d p r i m a r y b a l a n c e , % o f G D P ). records.text: 1 Insights Market Narratives in Focus: AI strength vs Macro Strain 18 May 2026 Equities. At a high level, equity returns have only two drivers: earnings and multiples (how much investors are willing to pay for those earnings). Currently, earnings remain strong—thanks to insatiable AI demand—while multiples face potential pressure from the oil shock. Our Narrative Map suggests markets are far more focused on the earnings (and AI) story (top right quadrant, Figure 1). Meanwhile, macro variables—Fed policy, interest rates, global growth, and the business cycle— are all shaky and could trigger multiple contraction yet they sit in Unimportant Silence. Even oil—the root cause of the current shock—is dismissed as Unimportant Hype. This sentiment is mirrored in institutional investor behaviour: since the start of the war, investors have crowded into IT—where earnings remain resilient—while cutting exposure across most other sectors (Figure 2). Inflation is the most obvious near-term worry and coverage of the narrative is certainly crucial for USD performance. FX policy: We think the MAS is likely to keep its FX policy focus on mitigating upside risks to inflation, as it is currently driven by external factors. This is evident in the MAS's decision to increase the SGDNEER slope at its April meeting. Given the persistence of high oil prices, there is a risk of further tightening at subsequent meetings, which is why we retain a long bias on SGD against its NEER basket. On the other hand, the reduction in global energy supplies poses downside risks to growth, particularly since Singapore's economy is heavily reliant on regional and global trade. To counter this, we expect the MAS to maintain accommodative monetary conditions by keeping liquidity levels flush, which will help keep front-end SORA rates low. Additionally, we think safe-haven-seeking flows into Singapore are likely to continue, further contributing to the abundance of liquidity (Figure 5). records.text: 02:00 PM FOMC meeting minutes, April 28-29 meeting At its April meeting, the FOMC left the fed funds rate and the policy guidance in its statement unchanged. Presidents Hammack, Logan, and Kashkari dissented against the implicit easing bias in the standing policy guidance, while Governor Miran dissented in favor of a 25bp cut. Chair Powell said that the number of FOMC participants who could support moving to balanced guidance has increased since March and that the center of the FOMC “is moving toward a more neutral” outlook for future rate changes, but most felt making a change now was unnecessary. We pushed back our expectations for Fed cuts by one quarter to December and March. With energy cost passthrough likely to keep year-over-year core PCE inflation closer to 3% than 2% all year, we think that a combination of lower monthly inflation prints after the oil shock fades and further labor market softening will likely be needed for the FOMC to cut this year. We still expect that bar to be met but now expect it to take a bit longer. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear 1518/05/2026 Supply to remain flexible: Unlike many other economies, Singapore often runs budget surpluses (Figure 9, overleaf), which gives the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) flexibility to adjust its auction sizes based on its assessment of what the market needs. The MAS can also conduct ad hoc mini-auctions or bond syndications if it deems them necessary. Gross and net supply: We expect bond supply in Singapore to remain stable in 2026, with gross issuance similar to previous years, based on the indicative calendar published by MAS. Net supply should also remain steady (or decline slightly), with about SGD21.6bn in maturities this year. Although Singapore’s fiscal year runs from April to March, the MAS releases its auction and issuance calendar by calendar year, typically in October or November of the previous year. It also publishes separate issuance calendars for MAS Bills and Floating Rate Notes (FRNs) semi-annually, in May and November. Bond curve seasonality: Auctions are typically held once a month, at month-end, with issuance taking place at the start of the next month, and typically very few auctions in November or December. The government tends to hold its last long-end auction in Q3, creating a gap in long-end supply towards the end of the year. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 620/05/2026 Cobalt: Prices to stay elevated Prices reach our forecasts: In Battery metals outlook: Beyond the soaring prices, dated 1 December 2025, we were bullish on prices in Q1 2026 given low inventories of feedstock and salts, but expected gains to be capped by reverse smelting of large cobalt metal stockpiles into cobalt sulphate, and by shipments out of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Prices indeed rose gradually in Q1 as inventories depleted, reaching USD25.86/lb, just shy of our end-quarter forecast of USD26.20/lb. However, the rise was not dampened by incoming supplies from the DRC, but by weak demand from EVs since December . Battery demand growth slows: Batteries still account for around 75% of cobalt end- use demand, mainly from the use of ternary batteries such as nickel-manganese- cobalt (NMC) or nickel cobalt aluminium (NCA) chemistries, on which Europe and the US have been more reliant. However, given policy changes in the US and surging cobalt prices, we see US EV sales waning while European automakers slowly shift towards the more cost-effective (non-cobalt) LFP batteries for mass -marketmodels . Chinese exports of both LFP and NMC batteries to Europe have risen as EV sales in Europe gain momentum, but LFP has seen the more dramatic surge since July 2025. As a result, we now expect headline inflation to rise to 3.4% in Q2 and look for core inflation to peak at 2.7% in Q2 (vs 1.9% before the war). 6. That said, we still see modest second-round inflation effects. The labour market remains resilient but is loosening given sluggish employment growth (at 0.1% in Q1), a declining vacancy/unemployment ratio and gently rising unemployment (for example, in France). While some forward-looking wage indicators (such as wage expectations in the ECB corporate telephone survey) have increased, they continue to show wage growth falling back into the 2.5-3% we see as consistent with inflation at target. We therefore expect core inflation to return to 2% by the end of 2028. 7. What 'Manchesterism' Means for the UK On May 15, Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham received the green light for a potential return to Westminster. To be sure, financial markets have rarely given such attention to by-elections. This one, however, will matter, with hugely consequential implications for macroeconomic policy. Indeed, Burnham's return as an MP could set in motion a shift in the Labour leadership towards the soft-left of the Labour Party. In this blog, we look at what a national 'Manchesterism' agenda could look like – building on the principles set out by the Greater Manchester Mayor. We highlight five pillars that could shape the near future of UK politics. What is 'Manchesterism'? Andy Burnham has spent nine years building something in Greater Manchester. But what is 'Manchesterism'? Burnham himself defined it plainly: "a distinct economic and political model rooted in devolution, long-term planning, and good growth ... a deliberate response to the high-inequality, low-growth trap Britain fell into from the 1980s onwards, when power was over-centralised in Westminster and key public institutions were fragmented or privatised." records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 What's Topical: Morgan Stanley's Global Views Global Macro Views Here we summarise Morgan Stanley's 2026 Global Mid-Year Outlooks, but please refer to Global Economics Mid-Year Outlook: A Fluid Outlook and Global Strategy Mid-Year Outlook: Constructive, Not Complacent, and more detailed country and asset-class reports. Energy and commodity markets, policy choices, and the speed of AI adoption all combine to define growth through 2027. In the baseline, the energy shock slows the global economy modestly through mid- 2026 before growth stabilizes and recovers into 2027: Morgan Stanley sees growth near potential across most major economies. AI-driven capex and fiscal spending on energy security and defense provide a firm floor to prolong late-cycle growth. Our global team assumes that the conflict in Iran is resolved in the next month, limiting the effects to one quarter, and that volatility from energy prices subsides over the balance of the year. While oil and gas prices push headline inflation higher in 2026, pass-through to core inflation remains limited in most economies: By 2027, those effects should fade, and combined with somewhat slower growth this year, underlying inflation should soften again. Against this backdrop, monetary policy must spend much of 2026 wrestling with the energy shock before a convergence toward neutral in 2027. As we show in Figure 15, a number of countries have sizeable aggregate debt to GDP , but a positive net international investment position – for example Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Belgium or Finland. Should a strong NIIP diffuse worries about high debt? Yes, to some extent, as foreign assets can potentially be liquidated to service debt. However, caution is required, particulary in case of high public debt. Foreign assets are usually held by the private sector or by the central bank (ECB/Eurosystem), but not by the government. Hence, in times of sovereign debt problems, governments can find it difficult to liquidate foreign assets. Governments could impose a one-off wealth tax on their citizens, but this would likely be politically contentious and it might not be possible to do this quickly. (2) Hence a strong NIIP might not always be able to diffuse sovereign debt problems (see also Annex, Figures 161-202). records.text: ab 18 May 2026 Global Research European Economic Perspectives Eurozone: Fiscal policy in 2026 – takeaways from budget plans 2026 annual progress reports provide updated fiscal projections... Fiscal stimulus in the form of higher defence spending across the EU and higher infrastructure spending in Germany is a key theme for the European macro outlook in the next two years. As usual in April, EU governments have submitted their budget plans to the European Commission, providing an update to 2026 fiscal projections. These plans used to be called stability programmes but are now called annual progress reports under the reformed EU fiscal framework. In this note, we review and aggregate the individual country plans, which show budget deficit increases in around half of Eurozone countries, including much higher deficits in Germany and Greece, and more mixed developments elsewhere. Croatia has not (yet) published its report and hence we use projections from the latest IMF Fiscal Monitor. ...showing moderate fiscal easing, heavily dependent on Germany Overall, we draw three key conclusions: (1) The updated budget plans point to moderate fiscal easing in the Eurozone in 2026 of 0.2% of GDP (in cyclically adjusted terms), slightly less than our (and the ECB's) expectation for 0.3% of GDP , but higher than the 0.1% of GDP assumed in the latest IMF Fiscal Monitor. records.text: . And when growth agendas are set via a bottom-up localised approach, good things happen. Why does devolution sit at the heart of 'Manchesterism'? Devolution allows city- regions to set their own objectives – building better social and human capital while diminishing the notion of 'left-behind' places. If regionally elected mayors are given more power to define the local growth agenda, better outcomes follow. In short, 'Manchesterism' rests on the notion that devolution can allow the UK to fire on all cylinders. In principle, from a financing perspective, 'Manchesterism' would likely mean more fiscal devolution plus more predictable block funding, not just bigger local authority grants. In practice, this would mean accelerating Government plans for fiscal devolution, with mayoral control stretching to business rates, land-value capture, visitor levies, and longer-term regional investment powers, with less constant bidding back to Whitehall. This would also put in place greater focus for more multi- year settlement funding for city-regions, fewer ring-fenced grants, and more retention of locally generated tax bases, so local government can plan around transport, skills, housing, and regeneration as one system rather than as separate central-government programmes. The upside is simple. Better local accountability, for one. Two, streamlined project delivery. And three, policies better tailored to fit local labour markets and industrial structures. Homebuilder sentiment improved 3 points in May but at 37 this is still a low level. Higher input prices weigh on builders and geopolitical and monetary policy uncertainty hold back homebuyer demand. The FRB of New York services index improved in May but remained in contraction, while prices indexes were fairly stable. Active oil drilling rigs rose 5 to 415 in the week ending May 15, the third consecutive weekly improvement but we have seen limited evidence thus far that higher oil prices are yet translating into more drilling. Looking ahead to this week, the April FOMC minutes will likely reflect a modest hawkish shift toward a more neutral stance. Some non-voters likely supported removing the easing bias, with "many" participants potentially favoring the change. records.text: alised in Westminster and key public institutions were fragmented or privatised." It's hard to dismiss some of the headline impacts of 'Manchesterism'. Since the creation of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority, the city-region's economy has grown at an average of 3.1% annually (2015 to 2023) — more than double the national rate. And while national productivity has stagnated for much of the last decade and beyond, Greater Manchester has seen a strong increase in productivity – since 2015, average annual productivity growth has hit 2%. In 2024, 13,000 people left London for Greater Manchester against 11,800 going the other way: the first net reversal of that flow in living memory. What's driven some of the success in Greater Manchester that could be used as a blueprint for the UK? We view the third hypothesis—that new technologies have enabled a small n number of firms to leverage economies of scale and capture larger market shares—as the most compelling. Across advanced economies, concentration has risen more rapidly during periods of faster technological change. Consistent with this, productivity dispersion has widened following technology shocks, with frontier firms extending their lead—particularly in technology-producing sectors and in industries most transformed by new technologies, such as online retail. Profit margins have also risen in recent decades. How much of the increase is n connected to rising concentration? Over the past four decades, US firms have raised markups substantially, reflecting two main forces. First, higher incomes have reduced consumers’ sensitivity to price differences, leading them to compare prices less across sellers. We believe that the slowdown is largely due to the reduction in consumer goods trade-in subsidies; in Q2 last year those subsidies delivered the most pronounced boost to retail sales. Sales of goods covered by these subsidies (excluding autos) contracted by 6.9% y/y in April, down from the 8.1% y/y growth in March, marking the lowest print since August 2024, when China introduced the subsidies. Auto retail sales also declined further, falling by 13.8% y/y. However, sales of goods not covered by subsidies (excluding jewelry) grew by 1.3% y/y, slightly above the 1.1% y/y increase recorded in March, indicating that organic consumption momentum has been stable. Property going through the last 10 % of downturn: Beyond a double-digit decline in property investment, new starts fell 26.6% y/y in April. Although sales volume slipped 9.5% y/y, it was slightly better than the 10.4 % fall in Q1. That said, the March rebound in second-hand housing prices continued: prices rose 0.4% m/m in tier-1 cities, the second consecutive month of positive growth. Prices in tier-2 cities stayed flat, compared with a 0.1% m/m decrease in March, while prices in tier-3 cities dropped by 0.3% m/m, matching March’s dip, due to higher inventories . The divergence across cities corroborates our view that the property sector is still going through the last 10% of the downturn, before reaching the bottom. records.text: arize that deposit increases on net basis when either BoJ or banks buy JGBs, that is, extending credit by banks. Conversely, deposit decreases in net term when either BoJ (QT) or banks reduces JGB positions. This mechanism of deposit creation/reduction is the same when banks extend loan to private sector also (Figure 6, right hand side). The dfference is that deposit creation is instant when credit is extended to private sector while there is a lag when extended to the government. Between 2022 and 2024, banks reduced JGB holdings as they expected interest rates to rise, while the BoJ was still buying JGBs under YCC (yield curve control), Then after 2024, BoJ reduced JGB holdings while banks as a whole offset some (Figure 7). Therefore, in net terms, we can say that the deposit reduction by the BoJ’s QT since 2024 was partly offset by banks’ JGB buying. To be sure, even though banks like to have deposit, they do not buy JGBs to keep deposit. Therefore, we think that “overfunded” JGBs is another source of fall in deposit, even though it is in theory “temporary”. In addition to such time lag, we also think there is a path where the deposit may not be recovered. In the path shown in Figure 4, we assume that the fiscal money is spent domestically, so either households or corporations receives the money in their deposit. Last week, Burnham cleared the first two obstacles: the resignation of Labour MP Josh Simons enabled Burnham to announce his intention to stand in the upcoming by-election, and the party’s National Executive Committee approved Burnham’s participation. However, Burnham still faces one hurdle before returning to Parliament: winning the by -election. A typical timeline would suggest 18 June is the earliest possible voting date, but Burnham’s prospects here remain uncertain. Polls from the constituency had indicated a strong performance by the Reform UK party at the next general election. Only when Burnham is again an MP can he launch a challenge against the prime minister. Our regressions control for time and industry fixed effects to isolate the impact of changes in concentration from aggregate business cycle dynamics and time-invariant industry characteristics. We estimate that on average across US industries, rising concentration accounts for roughly one-third of the increase in profit margins over this period (Exhibit 9). In turn, the rise in profitability at dominant US firms helps to explain elevated levels of equity market concentration. One factor that complicates the link between rising concentration and rising profit margins is that national-level concentration trends may overstate the decline in competition faced by US consumers.9 Across many local markets—particularly in retail trade, financial services, and food and accommodation services—larger firms have increasingly entered areas once dominated by a few small local incumbents. This can reduce local concentration—a town gaining a national retailer alongside its local store has now more competition than before—even as the rise of the national chain increases concentration at the national level (Exhibit 10). But the ultimate effect on profitability is hard to gauge. While the entry of large firms tends to reduce local concentration initially, it can also drive out smaller rivals over time, allowing the surviving firms to operate with wider margins and exert greater product- and labor-market power. 9 Rossi-Hansberg,

records.text: d bias in front-end AUD rates, as the RBA is in the midst of its hiking cycle. Inflation concerns that resurfaced in late 2025 have intensified in recent months due to rising energy prices. The RBA has delivered three back-to-back rate hikes so far, and markets are pricing in approximately one more rate hike this year. This seems reasonable to us, and we think risk–reward does not look attractive to pay at these levels. With the RBA signaling a potential pause at its next meeting in June, the next rate hike could be in August. However, as it remains only partially priced (June/Aug RBA trading around 16.5bp), we think this may be attractive to pay if it dips further. Over the medium term, we think long-end AUD could be attractive to receive against other DM rates – once the RBA raises its cash rate to 4.60% or higher, which will likely mark the end of the hiking cycle. Long-end AGS continue to provide a higher yield than most DM peers, and we think Australia’s AAA credit rating could lead to outperformance in an environment of increased fiscal spending globally. records.text: Second, the timing of inclusion matches the arrival of new issues. While creation and redemption baskets are not directly observable, ETF holdings provide a close proxy. Focusing on LQD, we compare the daily number of security holdings (Figure 6, dark blue line) with the cumulative number of new issues (Figure 6, light blue line) between January and March 2026. The two series are highly correlated (98%): on issuance days, LQD holdings increase, indicating that new bonds are incorporated into ETF flows shortly after issuance – via creation baskets and ahead of index inclusion. On days without issuance, holdings remain broadly stable. The largest adjustment occurs on the first business day of each month, when the number of holdings drops, reflecting ETF rebalancing. Over the rest of the month, new issues are gradually added again. To be clear, we do not argue that ETF create baskets are the channel through which ETF managers acquire new issues, as we believe many receive allocations directly in the primary market. However, the size, direction and timing of flows point strongly to a significant share of ETFs incorporating new issues in their create baskets ahead of the index rebalancing. FIGURE 6. Administrative policy tightening was likely the key driver. Administrative loosening to reverse the slowdown is expected. April activity data surprised significantly on the downside. This year is the start of the 5 Year plan, having a strong start is a key policy goal. There were likely some front-loading activities in 1Q, especially in terms of state-led investments. After the strong start of the year, policy makers became more confident about the economic outlook. Administrative policy stance turned effective less supportive with greater emphasis on (1) not setting over ambitious economic goals and reaching them by making wasteful mega investment projects which tend to be debt intensive, and (2) over report data when these overly ambitious goals could not be achieved. At the same time, officials were told not to “sit idle” either. Therefore, the incentive facing officials on the ground is to “do something but not too much”. But the actual penalties imposed on officials recently have been tilted towards those who had wrongdoings, instead of no actions. This can potentially explain why despite the PBOC’s significant loosening of interbank liquidity, credit growth has been weak. These interventions have drained INR liquidity and the RBI has sought to offset this via open market operations (OMOs) to inject durable liquidity back into the system. Additionally, the government has conducted bond buybacks, which, in combination with OMOs, has helped decrease the net market supply of bonds (Figure 8, overleaf). Despite these efforts, bond yields have continued to rise over the last year, driven in part by a decline in structural demand for bonds. Growth concerns are bubbling under the surface. Indeed, the impact of US and Chinese growth coverage has a stronger relationship to USD changes than inflation at this stage, despite being in the Important Silence quadrant of our map. Interestingly, International Conflict as a media narrative has less impact than it once might have on USD movements, as does changes in coverage of Investor Sentiment. The tension between growth and inflation is sure to define policymaker reaction functions in the coming months. On this note, it is fascinating that the tone of coverage of the Federal Reserve has become the most hawkish of the major developed market central banks in recent days (Figure 4). Thought to have the easiest bias of these institutions, not least given the perceived dovish inclinations of incoming FOMC Chair Warsh, the current coverage tone of the Fed contrasts with the drops towards neutral for the Bank of England and ECB, both considered locks to hike rates during the summer. Meanwhile, coverage of the Bank of Japan continues to hold a dovish tinge, emblematic of a central bank well aware of the inflation risks at present, but one reluctant to do much about it. records.text: 2 Japan Viewpoint | 18 May 2026 Parsing through the fiscal noise Japan’s fiscal debate has produced a steady stream of headlines over the past few months. Much of the attention has focused on proposals ranging from consumption tax cuts and cash handouts to a refundable tax credit system, an early supplementary budget, and changes to the fiscal framework. The resulting noise has made it difficult to form a coherent view of where fiscal policy is actually heading. The underlying structure is simpler. What appears as a fragmented set of debates is better understood as two negotiations running in parallel. One is structural reform of household income transfers, with a political contest over which “bridge” instruments should cover a multi‑year build‑out. The other is a separate negotiation over Japan’s fiscal framework. Most of the daily newsflow falls into one of these two buckets. The structural reforms at the center of both debates make sense as long run improvements to Japan’s fiscal policy. The risk lies in how they are delivered in practice. Choices made this year will shape Japan’s fiscal path well beyond any single budget. The two debates Debate 1: Structural reform of household income transfers + bridge negotiation The first debate, and the one driving most of the news flow, concerns structural reform of household income transfers. records.text: ab 18 May 2026 Global Research Global Equity Strategy The Consumer: be selective We look at consumer plays in Europe, US and China. Our concerns about the European consumer. There are several headwinds for the European consumer. First, even if the conflict ends tomorrow, we are left with gas at elevated price levels (120% above pre-conflict scenario in Q4 26), oil at 40% above pre- conflict scenario in end-26 (each 10% on oil takes 0.2% off consumption), food being affected by fertiliser prices (we are at peak planning season and if fertiliser prices are up c30%, then this leads to a c10% increase in food prices, adding c0.5% to CPI) and potentially higher rates (UBS forecast 2 rate hikes compared to none pre-conflict and we estimate each 50bps on rates taking 0.3% off consumption). The offset would be fiscal gifts to the household (which appear to be tiny compared to 2022/3), dis-saving (with current savings ratios being abnormally high) and slightly higher wage growth (though the ECB wage tracker shows little sign of this). Thus, we think it is quite feasible that consumption is c1%+ lower than pre-conflict estimates. Even employment growth has faded, running at just 0.1% QoQ in Q1 and 0.5% YoY in EZ and is negative in the UK. The consumer sectors, particularly retailing, outperforms when the Euro or Sterling strengthen (as typically they have more dollar costs than revenues). Storage demand has been muted, driven by relatively low levels of housing turnover. However, housing turnover has stabilized which should help limit further occupancy downside. At the same time, self storage supply is moderating but lingering at relatively elevated levels. Thus, we think more certainty around demand is needed to become more positive on the space. We view the current risk/reward as balanced for PSA. Michael Goldsmith on BXP: We have a Neutral rating on BXP . In our view, BXP faces a challenging leasing outlook due to increased uncertainty in the macro environment – particularly as companies contemplate slower hiring due to AI efficiencies. We believe BXP’s portfolio of high-quality buildings in top markets should outperform others. Still, demand trends have been mixed, leasing activity is spotty, and pricing power remains muted. Further, elevated capex spend is needed to maintain building quality and attract tenants. We think the risk/reward is balanced for BXP . A second constraint is legislative. Because a refundable tax credit requires tax legislation approved by both houses of the Diet, the LDP-Ishin coalition will in practice need cooperation from at least one opposition party to deliver the reforms. 1 This has turned the choice of bridge instruments into the political price for advancing legislation that the coalition cannot pass on its own. 1 Article 59 re-passage by a 2/3 Lower House majority is technically available: LDP holds 316 of 465 Lower House seats after the February 2026 election. In practice, this path is rarely used. The Upper House can hold a bill without voting on it, forcing the Lower House to wait 60 days before re-passing – a binding constraint within limited Diet session time. Ramming through legislation also carries a political cost, particularly heading into the July 2028 Upper House election.

Seasonally, there is typically a fall in net bond supply around the transition from one fiscal year to another. This is due to reduced issuance in March and sizable maturities in April (Figures 4 and 7). SDL issuances: The issuance of state government bonds, also known as State Development Loans (SDLs), has on the rise in recent years (Figure 9). The combined gross bond supply for both the central government and states is expected to total INR30trn in FY2026/27 (Figure 9). The latest budget has maintained the tax share for states at 41% for 2026-2031, which is likely to result in continued reliance on SDL issuance to meet their funding needs. OMOs and buybacks: The INR has faced depreciation pressures in recent years, forcing the RBI to intervene in FX markets. These interventions have drained INR liquidity, and the RBI has sought to offset this by conducting open market operations (OMOs) to inject durable liquidity back into the system. Additionally, the government has conducted bond buybacks, which, in combination with OMOs, has helped decrease the net market supply of bonds (Figure 8). Despite these efforts, bond yields have continued to rise over the last year, driven in part by a decline in structural demand for bonds.

Across the region, our analysis reveals a general trend of increasing gross bond supply in most countries, with current fiscal year levels surpassing those of previous years. We also investigate seasonal patterns in bond issuances and maturities, based on past auction schedules and outstanding bonds in the market. We also outline any market dynamics that may be unique to individual bond markets, such as Singapore, which issues bonds based on its assessment of market needs rather to finance deficit spending. Furthermore, we assess the effects of central bank activities, such as quantitative easing/tightening (QE/QT) measures and open market operations (OMO), on the duration and net supply to the market. Notably, we see that central banks in countries where rates have faced updated pressure in recent years have tended to provide support to the bond market through auctions and OMOs. In addition, we analyze the composition of government bond buyers and holders, including foreign ownership and recent trends. The relevance of this analysis has increased significantly in the wake of the Middle East conflict, as many Asian countries have maintained fuel subsidies or price caps to mitigate the impact of rising energy prices, such as Malaysia and India. records.text: EM – LOC AL EY ES F OR A GLOBAL VI EW 720/05/2026 Cobalt: Supply remains the largest concern Sulphur disruption: While the focus in the commodities space since the Middle East conflict has clearly been on oil and gas, second-order risks from curtailed sulphur supply are feeding through into cobalt production . Sulphur is a key input in the acid-leaching process by which cobalt ions are extracted from copper-cobalt or nickel-cobalt ores to produce intermediate products such as mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP) from Indonesia or cobalt hydroxide intermediates from the DRC. Additionally, sulphuric acid is used in the synthesis of cobalt sulphate – the main salt used in NMC-cathode manufacturing – from cobalt intermediates . Sulphur, however, is a by-product of oil and gas refining, making the Middle East one of the biggest producers and exposing trade in sulphur to the significant supply-chain disruption seen since the outbreak of hostilities (see Middle East conflict: Second- order effects on commodities, dated 20 May). We see a greater risk in Indonesia as over 70% of its sulphur imports are from the Middle East – we would expect increased costs or a physical sulphur shortage to reduce its cobalt production . Due to the DRC export restrictions, Indonesia has become effectively the leading supplier of cobalt to China . An increase in the AFP hedging ratio would support the CLP, lower FX points and compress the CLP basis (see Chile: Pension fund hedging shift to stabilize CLP basis , 17 September). Based on our latest estimate of AFP hedging positions (Figure 6), there is still capacity to increase hedging (though more limited than in past months). We do not anticipate it becoming the primary driver of USDCLP movements or of the CLP basis. In the short term, oil - price swings — still highly volatile — will keep driving USDCLP. Over the medium term, a prolonged period of elevated oil prices (our baseline scenario) remains a drag on the CLP. Nonetheless, the peso’s strong terms of trade (bolstered by robust copper prices), improved carry (as markets factor in rate hikes), and any extra hedging activity by AFPs could gradually reverse its recent underperformance — provided there isn’t another fresh significant surge in oil prices. Regarding the CLP basis, recent USDCLP volatility has turned the basis into a proxy for FX levels (Figure 7), and we anticipate this relationship to persist in the short run. Since the AFP - hedging utilization ratio is already above its long - run average (Figure 8) — though a strong CLP sell - off could lift it further — the room for additional AFP - driven CLP - basis compression is more constrained than in recent months.

Specifically, two key risk-mitigation metrics are being introduced: 1. LED (Maximum Derivative-Exposure Limit): Defined as the estimated loss of the fund’s derivative portfolio under stressed market conditions, expressed as a percentage of the fund’s total assets. 2. RCL (Liquidity Coverage Ratio): Defined as the amount of liquid assets available (by currency group) divided by the potential liquidity demand created by derivative operations in that currency group. AFPs have 210 days to meet both requirements (What are the specific requirements, expand and explain, refer to Fig 1). During the first 120 days, any excess is limited to a maximum of 40% above the thresholds. In this note we focus on the LED metric—because public data on the RCL are limited—and examines how the new limit could affect local assets (Camara, USDCLP, and the CLP cross-currency basis). The introduction of Bank Indonesia Rupiah Securities (SRBI) in late 2023 has had a significant impact on the Indonesian government bond (IndoGB) market, offering an attractive carry with lower duration risk. As a result, SRBI attracted substantial foreign inflows from late 2023 to 2024, as investors sought to reduce duration exposure during a period of rising interest rates. However, when Bank Indonesia began cutting rates, foreign investors shifted their focus to IndoGBs. Recently, with markets anticipating potential rate hikes following the tightening of BI's 7-day repo rate, the relative appeal of SRBI to IndoGBs has increased, prompting investors to seek lower-duration exposure. Although SRBI has attracted some foreign inflows in 2026 due to its attractive carry (Figure 10), we believe its support for the Indonesian rupiah (FX) may be limited, as most of these inflows are foreign exchange-hedged, mitigating their impact on the currency. Gross and net supply to increase: Gross bond supply is expected to rise from AUD102.3bn in FY24/25 to AUD127.5bn in FY25/26 (Figure 1). As a net commodity exporter, Australia's bond supply is often revised downwards when commodity prices surge, such as the current environment now, due to higher-than-expected tax receipts. Net bond supply is also set to rise, to AUD44.7bn for FY25/26 (Figure 3). However, net bond supply to the market is expected to increase by more, to AUD83.4bn this fiscal year, as AUD38.7bn of bonds are expected to mature on the Reserve Bank of Australia’s books. RBA purchases: The increase in net market supply can be attributed, in part, to the RBA’s balance sheet dynamics. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the RBA implemented quantitative easing measures, which involved significant bond purchases (Figure 5 overleaf). Since February 2022, the RBA has ceased making new bond purchases and has adopted a passive approach, allowing the existing bonds on its balance sheet to mature without replacement. PMIs reinforce this concern and reflect GDP estimates that are falling alongside ongoing negative economic surprises.  Earnings: Downgrades coming - Analysts have raised energy, materials and semis EPS forecasts dramatically but elsewhere, downgrades are modest but persistent. 2026 EPS growth that is now forecast to be 16% seems unlikely when input prices are surging for many large European sectors.  Valuations: No support - Valuations have moved in-line with bond yields that are rising. Valuations offer less protection against potential earnings disappointment than earlier in the year.  Sentiment: Fund flows have stopped - Three years of performance driven by lower bond yields and rising inflows has ceased. For Europe to rally now, earnings must grow. To be appealing relative to other regions, earnings must grow faster than other regions. records.text: China Economic Comment18 May 2026 ab 3 Retail sales decelerated to 0.2% YoY from 1.7% in March, contracting by -6% MoM Saar on a sequential basis. The April reading missed Bloomberg expectation of 2% YoY. The weakness was mainly due to goods retail sales, while catering sales growth slowed only modestly YoY. Among major products, sales of communication appliance decelerated notably, and sales of gold/silver/jewelry turned into YoY contraction. Sales of petroleum products declined by -6.5% YoY despite a low base, partly reflecting the impact from higher oil prices. Unemployment rate edged down seasonally, and stayed largely stable after seasonal adjustment. Exports beat expectation again in April. Export growth accelerated to 14.1% YoY in April, compared to the prior 2.5% YoY and expectation (BBG average 8.4%/UBSe 12%). We estimate the seasonally adjusted export levels expanded by around 2.4% MoM in April (32% MoM Saar) following a nearly 1% contraction in March. Sequential shipment to most destinations expanded. Shipments of tech exports expanded further sequentially (0.5% MoM), despite already strong gains in March and earlier months. Non-tech exports also saw broad-based strength. Meanwhile, import growth moderated to a still resilience pace of 25.3% YoY in April, compared to 27.8% in March, while its sequential growth stayed strong (54% MoM Saar). Although IG trades are typically agreed upon and executed based on spreads relative to a maturity-matched Treasury benchmark, these spreads are not reported to TRACE. Therefore, we used prices. For each bond and each day, we determined the difference between the average price of client buy trades, weighted by notional, and the average price of client sell trades, weighted by notional. We then averaged these differences across all bonds to obtain a daily bid-offer value, and normalised by the average client buy price to express bid-offer in percentage terms. This is computed separately for month-end and each day after issuance. Our own projection for the Eurozone fiscal stimulus this year is 0.3% of GDP , partly reflecting our expectation that there will be less discretionary tightening in France, Italy and Spain than assumed in their published budget plans. The overall Eurozone fiscal impulse crucially depends on Germany delivering on its large fiscal package; in fact, if the German CAPB were to remain unchanged, the overall Eurozone fiscal impulse would be slightly contractionary. Hence, closely watching the German budget execution is crucial – we do this regularly with our German fiscal stimulus tracker , which shows a sharp rise in federal spending in Q1, driven by defence spending. How much additional GDP growth will a 0.2% of GDP fiscal impulse generate? Assuming an average fiscal multiplier of 0.9, the budget plans indicate that fiscal policy will lift Eurozone GDP growth by c.20bp in 2026 (we assume 30bp in our forecast). But in the US, the debate on where “neutral” is will gain steam over the rest of this year and into next. US growth is supported by AI-driven capex and household spending. fueled by wealth effects: Consumption is expected to soften in coming quarters as energy prices weigh on disposable income, though underlying consumption trends remain robust. Immigration restrictions and lower labor force participation from demographics have pulled the “break- even rate” for job creation to ~50k/month, about one-fifth of the pace of early 2023. As economic growth broadens and hiring increases modestly late this year and next, the unemployment rate should move modestly lower over 2027. AI-driven capex is forecast to continue, but over time we expect investment to broaden to non-AI business fixed investment. In the case of a persistent oil price above $150/bbl, both consumer and business spending would slump. In the rest of the world, the inflation forecast is very sensitive to energy prices, even with Morgan Stanley assuming a rapid de-escalation. Morgan Stanley expects exports from the Gulf to carry a risk premium as production normalizes: Where AI is a dominant swing factor in the US, energy is the dominant swing factor in Europe; Asia is exposed to both trends to differing degrees. That being said, we think that near-term EGB issuance could lead to some modest widening of sovereign rates versus swap rates as EGB issuance is running slightly below its 3y average, but we did not pick up material concerns on US or EUR funding markets in recent client meetings. German 30y yields (at 3.66%) are trading 40 bps above 30y EUR swap rates (at 3.26%), with the spread 17 bps higher year-to-date. UK 10y not a buy yet - Receiving June 'BoE We have been telling clients not to go long UK 10y bonds as we think that political risks had been underpriced. The lesson from the mini budget of Liz Truss is that UK rates can price sharply higher on political uncertainty. There is more: the UK is an energy importer with inflation running above target for a while, so the bond market is also especially vulnerable to higher oil prices or higher US rates. Clients have been asking how much gilt yields could reprice in response to political developments. As a reference point, we estimate that around 90bps of additional term premium was priced into 10-year gilts in 2022 following Liz Truss’s mini-budget. However, at that time the BoE was in the middle of a rapid tightening cycle, which was also pushing up long-term rate expectations. records.text: one more rate rise during the summer. Several Governing Council members—including Bundesbank President Nagel—have stated explicitly that a rate hike in June will be appropriate unless the inflation outlook improves significantly. Others—including President Lagarde, Executive Board member Schnabel and Chief Economist Lane—have sounded more balanced, emphasising the need to see more data. But Lane reiterated this week that a mid-size shock (like the current one) probably warrants “some measured” policy tightening. We thus maintain our forecast for 25bp hikes in June and September. 8. Risks around our forecast run in both directions. The Governing Council might still decide to remain on hold (or hike only once) if energy prices fall sharply on the back of a US-Iran peace agreement, although the passage of time makes this less likely as pipeline inflationary pressures build. At the same time, a renewed spike in energy prices or emerging signs of second-round inflation effects could push the ECB into several hikes this year. Our probability-weighted rate path peaks at about two hikes, below market pricing for three rate rises. records.text: Timothy Graf20 May 2026 1 Insights Classification: Complimentary Material Developed Markets Strategy Weekly: Policy possibilities and dialing dollars to neutralKEY THEMES THIS WEEK: Policy trajectories shift. There can be no doubting the current behavioural set up for the US dollar: institutional investors are heavily underweight, but continue to sell with a degree of strength rarely seen. So it was not without significant debate that we close our two USD shorts this week, against NZD and NOK. Ongoing rate market volatility weighs heavily in our decision, as does the broader pricing for potential USD outcomes in FX option markets. Most importantly, the possibility that the Fed may soon have to join the ranks of the hawkish central banks ranks drives the main changes we make to our view set. Sentiment swings hawkish. It all comes down to who is priced to deliver rate hikes, who actually can deliver them and by how much. On this note, the fact that our measures of central bank coverage tone now show the Fed as having the most hawkish commentary of any G10 central bank sits at odds with the more modest tightening priced in the front end of the US rate curve over the next year relative to other central banks. It is not to say the Fed will necessarily outhawk the inflation-focussed ECB and BOE, but that it remains only marginally priced to do anything. We can compare such competitive situation vs. JGB market: Total supply of JGB market is fixed, but if investors do not have much demand, then the price has to fall until supply/demand matches. records.text: ta represents the average daily market spread based on quotes taken every 30 seconds in the order book aggregated across EBS and Reuters on a volume weighted basis. The spread signal is calculated as the ratio of the current spread relative to the prior one-year median spread. The values are then smoothed using a 20-day moving average. Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. records.text: Lisheng Wang +852-3966-4004 | lisheng.wang@gs.com Goldman Sachs (Asia) L.L.C. China: April activity data missed expectations broadly 18 May 2026 | 1:43PM HKT Bottom line: China’s activity data broadly weakened in April and missed market expectations meaningfully, reflecting the impact from the global energy-supply shock to the Chinese economy. Industrial production (IP) growth fell to 4.1% yoy in April from 5.7% yoy in March despite stronger-than-expected exports, mainly weighed down by slower output growth in chemicals and electric machinery industries. On a single-month basis, fixed asset investment (FAI) growth plunged to -8.2% yoy in April from +1.6% yoy in March, with weakness broad-based across sectors on the back of softer credit demand and heavy rainfall in southern China. Retail sales growth declined notably to 0.2% yoy in April from 1.7% yoy in March, with year-on-year growth in goods sales and restaurant sales revenue both weakening. The services industry output index growth – which is on a real basis and tracks tertiary (services) GDP growth closely – also slowed to 4.3% yoy in April from 5.0% yoy in March, and we believe its still-wide gap with retail sales growth suggests that services consumption growth continued to outperform goods consumption growth. Weaker-than-expected April activity data adds conviction to our forecast that sequential growth should slow in Q2 vs. Q1. Therefore, we complement the turnover analysis by examining median net client activity for each business day after issuance and at month-end, and plot the results in Figure 5 (negative values indicate that clients are net sellers).1 We find that clients are net sellers immediately after issuance and again at month-end. The median bond records net client selling of $36mn on the day of issuance and $12mn on the following day, after which clients become net buyers albeit the absolute magnitude of positions is relatively small. At month-end, clients turn to net selling in a magnitude of about $8mn. Dealers intermediate these flows, warehousing bonds and gradually unwinding them throughout the month to other investors seeking to buy the paper, particularly index-trackers. For context, that would typically represent 10 days’ worth of oil and product exiting the Strait (pre-war). - As per Bloomberg data, there were 414 tankers located inside the Persian Gulf as of April 7th. This translates into roughly ~210m barrels of oil & products cargo capacity (assuming ~90% of DWT is used for cargo). For context, this represents about ~10 days of pre- war export volumes via the Strait. - Should the ceasefire result in a meaningful restart in traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the key focus for owners of these vessels will be ensuring safe transit out of the Persian Gulf. This is particularly important given that at this point, the long-term durability of the ceasefire appears uncertain, meaning the availability of exit windows cannot be guaranteed. - Should vessels be able to safely navigate the Strait due to agreement between the US and Iran, it will take some time to return to normal as shipping companies evaluate the risk of seeing their vessels stranded should the conflict flare up again. At least as important, the possibility that the Fed may soon join the ranks of the hawkish central banks ranks drives the main changes we make to our view set this week. Our MKT MediaStats indicators measuring the tone of coverage of the major central banks has made a marked shift in capturing the relatively hawkishness in commentary around the Fed (Figure 3), pushing beyond even the ECB, who we see as hiking twice this year, being priced for even more. It has also pushed beyond the reading for the Bank of England, which is heading the other way. We stay short GBP, not believing the MPC will be in a position to hike as much as priced, though we do reduce the risk down to one short versus JPY. Sell AUDNZD. We keep the long side of both USD trades. Norway, like the US, is experiencing a significant, positive terms of trade adjustment and Norges Bank has already reversed one of the two cuts it was able to squeeze in last year, with two further hikes almost fully priced by year-end. New Zealand will likely be in a similar position, in our view, and could codify as such as soon as next week’s policy meeting. Moreover, Kiwi rates have priced a forward change relative to Australia that is in no way reflected in the AUDNZD cross (Figure 4). The budget airlines have a huge cost advantage over the flag carriers, which at times of higher oil prices increases their cost advantages, acting as a barrier to entry to new competitors and forces the less efficient players to cut capacity much more quickly. records.text: Stanley Research These scenarios highlight the dilemma facing central banks: the disinflation path of 2026 has been interrupted, but the extent is uncertain. This fact is most clear in the Euro Area. The ECB seems set on hiking rates to anchor inflation expectations, but the hit to growth will likely exceed their forecasts. Inflation risks are acute in Europe, but the ECB is not alone in seeking more information. The BoJ has signaled caution in its stance against further information, though their caution is to pause and risks of a delayed rate rise. The Fed similarly indicated that it requires sustained declines in inflation before considering rate cuts, a delay versus before when expectations of lower inflation were enough. We expect disinflation to return in 2027, but central banks will wait until they have clear evidence of that trend. Energy and commodity markets, policy decisions, and the pace of AI adoption will shape growth through 2027. The challenge is to interpret how the cyclical effects of the energy shock interact with positive structural drivers of trend growth in major economies. Our baseline remains constructive, acknowledging that outcomes are more diverse and probabilistic than usual.

records.text: TRADE IDEA T R A D E I D E A 19/05/2026 1 FX: Close long EURGBP for a small gain We close the long EURGBP spot trade that was initiated on 6 May, exiting the trade for a small gain (0.37%; USD 37k). Going into local elections in the UK on 7 May, we viewed valuations and positioning as consistent with limited UK political risk premium in the cross. This created an asymmetry to the topside, we thought, given the risks of the Labour party’s leadership changing and the potential for a GBP-negative shift in policy. The election outcome made this change more likely, with the focus having turned to the pathway for Andy Burnham, a former Labour MP and now mayor of Greater Manchester, to replace Keir Starmer as prime minister. That said, Burnham on Monday ruled out any changes to the existing fiscal rules as well as an exemption for defence spending that he had previously put forward. At face value, this reduced possible GBP-negative tail risks surrounding potential future changes in policy, in turn going against our long EURGBP trade idea. With the earliest possible date for the Makerfield by-election the 18 June, and momentum going against the trade, we deem it prudent to close the trade for a small gain.
